MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege arising out of an apparent change that has been made in Hansard. This only came to my attention yesterday although the matter to which I have reference occurred on Monday of this week, April 24. You will recall, sir, that in his introductory remarks the hon. member for Laurier, in a preface to the raising of his grievance, made the following statement with reference to Bomarc missiles:
The government Is building two Bomarc missile bases in northern Ontario and northern Quebec which, in order to be operative, must be equipped with nuclear weapons-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: What page?

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: Page 3933, on the right hand side. A few moments later, as you will recall, I rose on a point of order in order to challenge the validity of that statement. I copied down the words he used and referred to them as found at page 3934. No reply was made to that statement of mine, and I was astonished yesterday to have it pointed out to me that in fact the word "operative" appears to have been changed to "effective". I am not suggesting for a moment that the hon. member made this change intentionally, but it would certainly seem to me that it would require some explanation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was discussing this motion the other day the hon. member rose on a point of order and said that he had taken down my words. The words which he took down were taken down erroneously. They were not the words I had used on the occasion in question.
I do not remember whether or not Your Honour was in the chair at the time, but I believe you were. However, Your Honour made it quite clear to the hon. member that he had no right to interrupt me at the time he did because he was not making a point of order but was challenging a statement I had made. Your Honour also made it quite
clear to him that if he wanted to challenge a statement made in the house he should follow the rules of the house and make a statement afterward. He did not choose to do that, but today he rises in his place on a question of privilege, four days after the occasion arose. I think the practice of this house, as you have ruled repeatedly, Mr. Speaker, is that when there is a question of privilege a member should rise immediately thereafter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: If I am correct in understanding the hon. member for York-Scar-borough, his question of privilege relates to the alleged change of the word "effective" to "operative".

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: It is the other way around.

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that the word "operative" was used, and upon being challenged later it now appears in Hansard as "effective".

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: That is in the remarks attributed to the hon. member for Laurier?

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER
speechtext: I am not sure that the hon. member's complaint is one that warrants attention after four days have elapsed. However, if the hon. member for Laurier wishes to comment on the alleged question of privilege arising from the change of the words, I shall be glad to hear him.

subtopic: MR. MCGEE    REPORTED ALTERATION IN "HANSARD" BY HON. MEMBER FOR LAURIER

speechtext:

Moreover, sir, the Prime Minister made no attempt to answer the very proper question I put to him. I merely asked the Prime Minister, and I did so in the politest way possible, whether an order in council had been passed of which the house had not yet been apprised. Questions may be placed on the order paper seeking information from ministers of the crown relating to public affairs; and from other members, relating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the house, in which such members may be concerned-
These are the words that I think have a special bearing with respect to the reply made by the Prime Minister:

speechtext:
I wish to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of news reports to the effect that the Laos team is


split on an understanding of its role and procedure, would the minister inform the house whether the Canadian members of the commission have received specific instructions in this respect, and also would he comment on the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the report in question is a bit premature, because the commission was not to meet until today. The key point in this whole Laos problem is whether or not there will be a cease fire in Laos. As I informed the house on April 25, the first step in the procedure agreed to by the co-chairmen at the Geneva conference, that is by the Soviet union and by the United Kingdom, for dealing with the critical situation in Laos was a call to the two parties in Laos for a cease fire. Both sides have accepted this call in principle.
Hon, members will recall, however, that representatives of the parties were requested by the co-chairman to enter into negotiations on, and I quote, "questions connected with the cease fire". In other words, the people who are fighting in Laos are to negotiate on that point. There has not yet been agreement in Laos, so far as I am aware, as to where or when such negotiations will begin. Continued delay in reaching agreement on this matter could have very grave consequences. I earnestly hope a satisfactory agreement will be reached promptly by the parties. Dispatches indicate that the fighting is still going on, in spite of the fact that everybody says we are going to have a cease fire.
If agreement is reached and a cease fire takes place, then the international supervisory commission, which is holding its first meeting in New Delhi this afternoon should, and I hope will, be able to begin immediately its task of verifying and supervising the cease fire, so the subsequent conference of 14 nations can be held as planned in Geneva on May 12.
The Canadian representatives on the supervisory commission have their instructions, and I am sure they will be doing their best to work amicably with the representatives of India and Poland. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, that does not mean that Canada will agree automatically to everything that is suggested by another member of that commission. These are rather complicated discussions and operations, and sometimes things are not as simple as they look on the surface in connection with the work of these commissions. But our objective throughout will be to help in every possible way to bring about a settlement of the troubles in Laos.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CO-OPERATION BETWEEN ONTARIO AND FEDERAL DEPARTMENTS IN OVERSEAS MARKETS
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, notice of which has been given. Would the minister tell the house the relationships which exist between his department under this government and the government of the province of Ontario in the interests of promoting trade jointly with overseas markets, and how the two departments are officially associated in this endeavour?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: CO-OPERATION BETWEEN ONTARIO AND FEDERAL DEPARTMENTS IN OVERSEAS MARKETS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I was sent notice of this question relative to a statement which was made yesterday by Hon. Leslie Frost, premier of Ontario, in this regard. We welcome the initiative of the province of Ontario in developing further specialized services, as expressed yesterday by its very able premier, Hon. Leslie Frost. I am particularly happy that these plans call for dovetailing with, rather than duplication of, the vigorous efforts being made by our trade commissioners abroad.
For many years our officers in the United Kingdom and on the continent of Europe, as well as in New York and Chicago, have worked in close co-operation with all provincial offices in important matters, particularly those concerned with the attraction of industry to Canada and matters of general trade development. As do other agencies, our trade commissioners constantly report new opportunities for Canadian exporters in these markets as well as in other parts of the world.
The close co-operation between my department and the provincial authorities has been exemplified by our export trade promotion conference in Winnipeg on February 6 and by plans for similar conferences in Calgary on May 16, in Vancouver on May 18 and in London, Ontario, on May 25. We look forward enthusiastically to further conferences in at least two other centres of Ontario and in other provinces-

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by informing the house about some of the most important aspects of the work of my department. It will be impossible to cover all the diverse and wide ranging responsibilities of this department. However, I would remind hon. members that the annual report of the department was tabled on April 14 last. In it they will find a comprehensive review of economic and trade developments affecting Canada as well as a great deal of detailed information on our departmental activities during the year 1960.
My remarks today will be divided into four broad categories. I shall begin with a review of our trade and economic situation and the outlook for the next few months. Next 1 will outline the department's work and achievements in the field of trade promotion. I shall then give some details on the subject of trade policy and, finally, I shall review some of our efforts on the domestic and commercial fronts.
During the past year, developments in the foreign trade field have provided strong underpinnings for activity in the Canadian economy, and a higher level of exports has added to production and employment in Canadian industries. Imports, meanwhile, have edged downward. The result has been a substantial improvement in Canada's trade balance. The deficit on merchandise trade declined from $369 million in 1959 to $97 million in 1960, the lowest figure since 1954. In I960 our merchandise exports reached $5,395 million, 5 per cent above the level for the preceding year. This followed a similar increase between 1958 and 1959.
Most of the expansion in exports in 1960 consisted of higher sales in various mineral products including pulp and paper, lumber, aluminum, nickel, copper, petroleum, asbestos,


iron and steel and chemicals. In addition, the various types of manufactured products have been sold in larger quantities. The progressive dismantling of import restrictions throughout the trading world has opened up new market opportunities for this type of export.
An outstanding feature of our export trade in 1960 was a substantial growth in sales to overseas markets. Between 1959 and 1960 our exports to the United Kingdom increased by 16 per cent; to the common market by 39 per cent; to Japan by 27 per cent, and to all overseas areas taken together by about one fifth. On the other hand, our sales to the United States declined by nearly 5 per cent. However, sales of all foreign goods in the United States market were down. Thus the relative position of Canadian imports in that market was pretty well maintained.
Imports into Canada in 1960 were slightly below the 1959 level and, in fact, were less than four years ago. Despite the difficult competitive position faced by some industries, total shipments from Canadian factories, in aggregate, have about kept pace with imports of manufactured goods. Domestic manufacturers, for the most part, have been able to maintain their relative position in the Canadian market, although there have been some exceptions.
Another notable feature of Canada's trade in 1960, and in fact for several years past, has been its growing geographic diversification. This has involved in particular a lessening concentration of trade with the United States and a growing relative importance of trade with countries such as the United Kingdom, West Germany and Japan. The steadily improving competitive position of overseas industrialized countries has enhanced their importance as sources of supply for the Canadian market. At the same time strong internal growth rates within these areas have involved sharply expanded markets for Canadian products. Reflecting these broad tendencies, the proportion of our exports going to the United States has declined from 62 per cent in 1959 to 56 per cent in 1960. This means that 44 per cent of our total exports now go to overseas markets. The geographic distribution of our imports remained almost unchanged between 1959 and 1960. However, during the last four years the United States share of the Canadian import market has declined from 73 per cent to 67 per cent, while the share enjoyed by overseas countries has risen correspondingly.
There is good reason to anticipate that the improvement realized in Canada's trade position in 1960 will carry forward in the current year. Export figures have been fluctuating sharply from one month to another, but for

the first two months of the current year our exports have held within 3 per cent of the record level achieved in the same months a year ago. Imports also are down moderately. In the January-February period the merchandise trade balance has shown little change from a year ago, with exports and imports near to an even balance.
Total exports have been maintained at a high level in recent months despite lower sales in the U.S. market. Economic activity in the United States has been declining, and in the first quarter of 1961 industrial production was at a level 8 per cent below the previous high point achieved in January 1960.
As usually happens, the adverse effects of this decline in factory output upon the demand for .ndustrial materials has been accentuated by inventory liquidation. In consequence Canada's sales to the United States, as reflected in export trade figures for the last three months, have recently been running 17 per cent below the level of a year previous. In the over-all trade figures, however, lower sales to the United States have been largely offset by increased shipments overseas. Recent signs of hesitancy in the trend of activity in some overseas countries have not, up to this point, affected the upward movement in our shipments to overseas markets.
The Canadian economy, and in particular the level of trade, cannot be fully insulated from the effects of economic fluctuations in major foreign market areas. Nevertheless, forward-looking action can help to cushion the adverse effects of these fluctuations. I have already illustrated how the recent broadening out of our markets has helped to limit adverse reactions emanating from the current down trend in the United States.
The manner in which higher exports to overseas markets has helped to cushion the shock of recession in the United States further emphasizes the vital importance of diversification of Canada's trade, and the continued expansion of trade with overseas countries.
Hon. members will already have seen the dominion bureau of statistics trade figures for February and for the cumulative Janu-ary/February period, which were released this morning. They reveal the fact that while our exports in the first two months of the year increased by 22 per cent to the United Kingdom, and by 37 per cent to other commonwealth countries, compared to the same period last year, a drop of 14.5 per cent in our shipments to the United States has caused a fall of nearly 3 per cent in our total exports to all countries. At the same time, while our imports from all other sources have increased, a reduction of just under
28, 1961
Supply-Trade and Commerce 6 per cent in our imports from the United States has helped to maintain an almost even balance in our over-all trade balance.
It would be difficult indeed to find more conclusive evidence than this with which to vindicate the policy of multilateralism in trade which this government has consistently followed. While dealing with what might be termed our chronic deficit in trade with the United States, it is imperative that our exports be vigorously expanded and that we continue to seek out new overseas markets for Canadian products.
There are other bright spots in the current trade situation. The careful attention which we have given in recent years to market potentialities in mainland China has now paid off in large new orders for wheat and barley. Perseverance in the development of this market by the Canadian wheat board and by our foreign trade service has been an important contributing factor in bringing a major portion of this new business to Canada. The development of advanced types of aircraft by the Canadian industry is now showing up in substantially higher aircraft exports. Canada's new national oil policy, calling for more rapid growth in this highly productive industry, is injecting new initiative into the development of export markets. The orderly development of new outlets for natural gas provides the basis for a continuing growth in exports of this product. A substantial addition to Canada's iron ore producing capacity brings with it new export outlets for this commodity. The growth of our sales of these and other items will help to offset the temporary ill effects of economic adjustment in the United States and possibly in some other countries.
There is also a general expectancy that an upturn in United States economic activity is now beginning or is close at hand. In this event we can look forward to underlying improvement in the United States market as the year progresses. Just the same, we are not standing by waiting for markets to get better. The Department of Trade and Commerce is continuously seeking out ways to stimulate export trade, and major efforts to this end have recently been initiated.
On August 5,	1960, at page 7666 of
Hansard, my colleague the former minister of trade and commerce, indicated certain changes in the organization and personnel of the department. At that time he forecast the appointment of two new assistant deputy ministers. As a result of interdepartmental examinations conducted by the civil service commission, assistant deputy ministers responsible for commodities services and domestic

Supply-Trade and Commerce commerce have been appointed. This reorganization has improved administrative efficiency and has enabled the department to move ahead boldly in two very important fields of endeavour.
One of our primary functions is to promote the sale of Canadian products in world markets. I think our record is one we can be proud of. Our export trade promotion conference, held in Ottawa from November 30 to December 16, was one of the most effective means ever employed to arouse the attention of Canadians and Canadian producers to the advantages and the value of our export trade. You will remember that when we brought back all the trade commissioners from abroad there were 110 of them here. Alert businessmen immediately recognized the advantages of meeting with these officers. In fact 1,365 Canadian businessmen, representing 1,133 Canadian firms, met for a total of 10,502 interviews with our trade commissioners.
It is still too early to give an accurate measurement of the results of those meetings. However, by the middle of March we had definite word from the trade commissioners that 344 new agencies or buying connections had already been established, and that there were good possibilities for upwards of 2,000 more. Trial orders, as a direct result of the meetings last December, have already been placed in 26 countries for Canadian goods valued at more than $1 million. As we do not know the value of many other orders, the actual total may well approach $2 million. The goods concerned include the products of agriculture such as, seed potatoes and baby chicks as well as flour and frozen foods. They include a wide range of manufactured products such as wood pulp and whisky, kitchenware and cutlery blanks, lamps and leather wallets. There were substantial orders for acetate, chemicals, electrical equipment, fibre glass cloth and leather.
The spirit of this export trade promotion conference continues with the hearty cooperation of provincial authorities and business associations. My senior officers and I participated in a regional trade promotion conference in Winnipeg on February 6, when more than 600 businessmen turned out for the discussions. On May 16 we have a similar trade conference coming up in Calgary. On May 18 there will be another one in Vancouver and on May 25 still another in London, Ontario. The provincial authorities and the businessmen who are organizing these meetings are most enthusiastic about the prospects. The departmental team from Ottawa is also finding these personal contacts with governments, business and industry across the country a rewarding experience

The trade commissioner service is the overseas arm of our department. During 1960 there were more than 120 trained officers in this sales force, stationed at 63 posts in 47 different countries. Quite apart from the special efforts connected with the export trade promotion conference, our trade commissioners were instrumental last year in establishing 847 agency or buying connections for Canadian export products. They also received and dealt with more than 9,000 inquiries from Canadian exporters about market opportunities and conditions abroad.
We are continuing to build this foreign sales force by means of an aggressive recruiting program. This year we have selected 15 promising young men who will shortly begin their training in the department. As the problems connected with international trade grow in number and complexity, greater demands are constantly made upon our resources of trained officers for special assignments and negotiation work. A large group of trade commissioners is now in Ottawa receiving training and experience in these fields.
One of our most important forms of export promotion is participation in trade fairs abroad, where Canadian goods are placed directly before the prospective agent and customer. Selection of fairs in department's program is made on the basis of active market possibilities. We show Canadian goods wherever there are good prospects that Canadian products can be sold. Results have been very encouraging. Since April 1, 1960 we have exhibited in 13 fairs outside Canada and by April 1, 1962 we will have participated in 17 more. Many of these are of a very specialized nature, because it is in the specialized fair that we find our best prospects.
We do not ignore the large, general shows, however. One such exhibition is the ideal homes show held in London in March each year. In 1960 the Canadian stand comprised 51 booths. This year it had expanded to 86 booths. No less than 36 of those who participated' in 1960 returned for this year's show. We shall continue to extend our participation in the important trade fairs of the world.
Trade missions are another proven medium for promoting trade. We have given them a specialized application by planning missions for very specific purposes and organizing them intensively to those ends. Here again results have been encouraging. The two missions which we sent to the United Kingdom last fall-one on timber and the other on processed food-are still bringing results, not only in the form of new business but in the continued interest of the members

of the missions who are working together to achieve improved methods and procedures. Our high level mission to the common market countries successfully achieved its immediate purpose of maintaining our exports of specific commodities. It has also had a continuing benefit, in that the leaders of industry who comprised the mission have met on several occasions since their return to discuss their impressions. The missions of consulting engineers and construction engineers which we sent to South America also give definite promise of new business abroad.
There are many risks attached to export operations which are not normally encountered in the domestic market and against which Canadian firms cannot obtain coverage through private sources. Here again the department, through the services of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, provides valuable assistance to Canadian industries by insuring them against non-payment by foreign buyers. Business done in 1960 was up 34 per cent over 1959. May I remind hon. members, Mr. Chairman, that the annual report of the corporation was tabled in the house last month.
Last November I announced in this house that the banks and the government were cooperating closely to provide financing for export sales of capital goods on credit terms. Just last week the banks announced the establishment of the Export Finance Corporation of Canada, Ltd., which has been set up to provide a new and separate source of funds for exporters selling capital goods to foreign buyers on medium term credit. Where long term credit extending beyond five years is required, the government is prepared to provide financing under section 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act. I made a statement in this connection in the house just two weeks ago outlining the very satisfactory developments and substantial figures involved.
Such aggressive measures to promote Canada's trade at home and abroad must be supported by closer liaison with industry in Canada. This is the lesson of recent experience. Twenty per cent of the firms which took part in the export trade promotion conference had no previous contacts with the department. Expansion of industry all across Canada in recent years and a new drive for industrial development in all provinces have stimulated a growing interest in the possibilities of export trade. Greater concentration of attention on aids to small business and domestic commerce is translated into new interest at the local business level in the services which are available from the department.
Thus the need to establish regional offices of the department to provide these services
Supply-Trade and Commerce more readily, and with greater continuity, is clearly apparent. As a consequence it has been decided to open regional offices in Halifax and Winnipeg in the near future. As soon as possible thereafter two more regional offices will be opened in Montreal and Toronto. At the same time our two existing offices in Vancouver and St. John's, Newfoundland, will be strengthened, to place them on a similar footing. In this way we hope to greatly increase the effectiveness of our assistance to industry and business across Canada and to provide closer liaison with provincial governments in the field of industrial development.
Let me now dwell on the department's activities and responsibilities in respect of Canada's international trade relations. In the light of the debate earlier this week on the government's trade policy, and the very complete review of our commercial relations contained in the department's annual report at pages 19 to 29, I do not intend to make a comprehensive review of this subject at this time. Members have been kept continuously informed in the course of the current session either by myself or by my colleagues.
Let me say briefly that our trade policy objective, to which we have constantly directed our endeavours, is to foster the development amongst trading nations of policies conducive to stability, growth and the expansion of mutually beneficial trade. In order for the very intensive export effort of my department and the business community to bring results, it is first necessary to have access to markets throughout the world on equal terms with our competitors.
This objective, in the main, has been realized. The handicaps under which dollar country exports laboured in the transitional period of post-war recovery have been largely removed since 1959, and together with the renewed economic strength of the major importing nations, exports have made very substantial gains.
The new stimulus which has been given to Canadian export sales as a result of the trade promotion conference places a further responsibility on the government. This department, in seeing that the conditions under which our goods move into international trade continue to improve, is therefore further intensifying its efforts to have import restrictions removed by those countries which no longer have balance of payments difficulties. I am confident that we can expect to see substantial improvements in this regard. I also look to some progress in this direction by less developed countries.
As the tide of trade restrictions recedes, the restrictive effect of agricultural protectionism abroad emerges as a problem of

Supply-Trade and Commerce major concern to Canada. Barriers to imports of agricultural products by other countries are a serious impairment to our trade, and we must press forward in restoring the balance of advantage between the agricultural exporting countries and their trading partners. We are convinced that there is room here for considerable reduction in tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade.
Meanwhile Canada is participating in the work of the GATT committee which is examining ways and means of expanding world agricultural trade. We are likewise active members of the international wheat agreement, as well as of the wheat utilization committee, for the expansion of world wheat consumption and trade. Similarly we take part in regular consultations with the United States authorities for the safeguarding of commercial markets for wheat. These interests continue to be fully taken into account in the formulation of our broad commercial policy.
The enthusiastic response of Canadian exporters for the development of trade has also meant that the government's constant efforts to safeguard and improve our access to all world markets take on greatly increased importance. These efforts consist of ensuring, first, that equitable treatment is accorded Canadian exports to those markets; second, that our competitive position in such markets is not impaired by the application of measures prejudicial to our exports; and finally, that commercial markets for our goods are not disrupted by our competitors, whether in the form of subsidies, surplus disposal programs or other means.
The government, through my department, plays an important role in keeping exporters informed of conditions in each market and the best means of exploiting them to advantage, in exploring new areas where trade may be developed, and by ensuring that our trade agreement relationships with all areas are soundly based. The negotiation of the new trade agreements with both Australia and the U.S.S.R. last year exemplifies our activities in the latter field. We are constantly reviewing possibilities for similar fruitful negotiations with other countries where commercial opportunities exist.
In our endeavours to seek out new opportunities for our exports and to defend our commercial interest, this department is fully conscious of the need to have a forward looking and flexible trade policy. We must look ahead and anticipate developments and changing conditions. With our dependence on exports we must keep all doors open and ensure that the most favourable conditions for multilateral trade are maintained. We must be constructive and ever mindful that we are on a course in our international trade
[Mr. Hees.l
relations which will contribute most effectively to our future economic growth.
I have spoken previously on the subject of regional developments in Europe, Mr. Chairman, but there are two points which I should like to make again at this time. The first is with regard to the common market and the E.F.T.A. group. Both have a collective obligation to ensure no less favourable access to their areas than previously existed. We will expect both groups to live up to this responsibility. The present negotiations with the common market on the level of the common tariff are approaching the final stages, and I am hopeful of a settlement which will be satisfactory from the Canadian point of view.
The emergence of both these communities will mean that we may have to make some adjustments in the pattern of our trade with Europe. On the other hand, in the expectation that our access will generally be not less favourable than before, and provided that, collectively, their trade policies will be outward looking, we need not be pessimistic about the growth of trade opportunities for Canada. Certainly our export results in Europe have been favourable to date.
The second point I wish to make is that we are about to enter the main round of tariff negotiations at the conference in Geneva, which will provide Canada with an opportunity to obtain better tariff access to markets throughout the world, including both the United States and the common market. This is another important step in the direction which this government intends to maintain for the betterment of our exports.
Finally, we have the possibility that the United Kingdom will become more closely associated with the common market. We have no clear indication as yet as to what may come out of the British initiative. However, we have indicated to the United Kingdom authorities the importance we attach to duty free and unrestricted entry to the British market for industrial materials and agricultural products, as well as to the preferences we enjoy, particularly in certain manufactured products. I can assure the house that this matter is being followed closely, and that we will see to it that no opportunity is lost to safeguard our commercial interests in whatever arrangement may eventually emerge.
It is essential to the objectives of the department that we seek continually to extend our knowledge of supply conditions in Canada, to widen our industrial contacts and to search for products and services which can be exported. These are the primary functions of our commodity branch which, by active liaison with industry, develops a continuing

exchange of commercial intelligence between posts abroad and industry in Canada. Active trade promotion programs carried on by this arm of the department have achieved success in many different directions.
We have placed sustained emphasis on the promotion of Canadian consulting engineering and construction services in foreign markets. Opportunities in markets abroad have been widened considerably for groups of Canadian consulting engineers through direct contacts arranged by the department with the international bank in Washington and the United Nations special fund in New York. This approach has resulted in an increase in exports of Canadian equipment, machinery and services. Noteworthy among these items has been equipment incorporating highly advanced design, such as telecommunications equipment, cargo aircraft, air navigation equipment and various types of automation equipment.
Let me just mention several notable successes. Specialty printing papers have been introduced into Australia, South Africa and Mexico, and fir plywood into western Germany. Gratifying results have also been obtained in stimulating increased timber sales in the United Kingdom. Substantial gains have taken place in exports of chemicals, metals and minerals. Encouraging results have recently been experienced in the promotion of manufactured consumer goods, particularly to the United Kingdom, in the wake of relaxed import controls.
Success continues to attend efforts of Canadian industry to re-establish itself in the United Kingdom market following the removal of import restrictions in 1959. Due to quality and design of the goods offered, excellent results have been achieved in the sale of synthetic and cotton fabrics, high-styled clothing for men and women, slippers, moccasins and jewelry. A concentrated effort is being launched by the Canadian food processing industry following the Canadian food trade mission to the United Kingdom last autumn. Very substantial sales of livestock and poultry products have been realized by our trade missions, and following visits to Canada by foreign trade delegations. The Latin American countries are showing a renewed interest in Canada as a source of supply.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn now to the domestic market. For a number of years after the war Canadian producers faced a minimum of competition in our home markets. In fact Canadian goods, both primary and manufactured, were shipped to markets all over the world. In more recent years, however, Canadian producers have faced increasing competition both at home and abroad. The
Supply-Trade and Commerce reason is that countries which until recently were markets for our products have completely recovered from the devastation of war and are now producing goods of excellent quality and design which sell at competitive prices.
This increase in competition has not always meant that we have lost markets, but it does mean that Canadian industry, in order to retain its markets, must also turn out goods of high quality and design at competitive prices.
To accomplish this task there must be co-operation among labour, management and government. All our energies must be directed to improving our competitive position. We must not dissipate our strength in internal disputes and strife.
To a very large extent the recovery of industry in Europe and Japan is directly attributable to the close co-operation of labour and management in those countries. This cooperation has been so effective that industry in these countries is now producing some of the best goods in the world, at prices which are extremely competitive.
The government has taken the lead in assiting Canadian industry to adjust to these changing conditions. Under the auspices of the departments of trade and commerce and labour, leaders of Canadian industry and commerce and top union officials were called to Ottawa recently to discuss ways of achieving greater co-operation in Canadian industry as an effective means of increasing Canadian output and improving our competitive position.

There was general agreement at that meeting that Canadian labour, management and government could work together to achieve the same results. Labour, management, government, and the general public are also combining their efforts through the national productivity council. The council has been meeting regularly and is developing an active program to assist Canadian industry in a variety of fields which will improve its ability to sell its goods in both home and

Supply-Trade and Commerce overseas markets. The chief objective of the council is to lend every assistance to Canadian industry in increasing its productive efficiency. The council is now enlisting the support of regional and provincial groups in order to carry this work to all parts of Canada.
At the same time we have established new services in the department and have expanded a number of our existing facilities in order to assist Canadian industry in meeting the new challenges which it faces. Over the last year we have built up a strong domestic commerce service whose function it is to provide assistance to industry over a wide range of the production and distribution aspects of business. We are now in a position to give information and help on such important subjects as product design, financing, new product possibilities, industrial development, distribution, sources of material, industrial standards, production under licensing arrangements and managerial and technical training and education. This is not by any means an exhaustive list. It is, however, indicative of the comprehensive services which we are developing to help Canadian business and industry.
Rapidly changing economic conditions have often posed difficulties for small businessmen. The government has recognized these difficulties and has taken steps to assist businessmen in overcoming them. A small business branch was established in the department to provide a focal point where the small business man could come to discuss his problems and obtain assistance and advice.
As I have often stressed, Mr. Chairman, we place very great importance on good design as one means of making Canadian goods as competitive as possible. With this in mind a national design branch has recently been established in the department. The function of this branch is to encourage the improvement of design in Canada, and to foster an awareness of the importance of good Canadian design. We have also introduced legislation providing for the establishment of a national design council.
The department has been increasingly active during the past year in the field of industrial development. The industrial development branch has increased its activities in new plant establishment, production expansion, product diversification, licensing arrangements, and other aspects of industrial development. It has also given valuable assistance to Canadian manufacturers in uncovering new markets for their products in Canada. Industrial development is further stimulated through special capital cost allowances administered by the department. In


all these endeavours the department is working very closely with the provincial department of trade and industry.
Another arm of the department is the dominion bureau of statistics. I need hardly remind hon. members that the bureau is acknowledged the world over as one of the foremost organizations in its field. During the past year it has kept pace with many complicated and highly technical developments. Its functions in providing statistical information and analyses have been widened and improved in response to demand. Its services to governments, industry and business in our country have been of incalculable value.
The most formidable task which faces the bureau this year is, of course, the 1961 census, which will be taken on June 1 next. This will be the tenth decennial census of Canada since confederation. The results of the census will provide a valuable national inventory of information on the composition of our population, the types of homes in which we live, the area and type of agricultural operations, and the size and nature of trade and service establishments operating in Canada. With the advantage of this up-to-date information about ourselves and our country we shall be better able to gauge our capabilities in meeting the challenges on the economic front which he ahead.
In conclusion may I say this. It has been a very full year for the Department of Trade and Commerce, a year of growth, of change and of achievement. We have made a contribution in the development of many new and important forces designed to strengthen our economy, expand production and increase employment in Canada. We have carried out organizational and administrative changes within the department which will ensure that we shall continue to provide the most efficient possible service to Canadian business and industry.
We find ourselves in the midst of a highly competitive and rapidly changing world economy. We face new and serious problems which must and will be overcome. At the same time we have great natural wealth, many natural advantages and, most important of all, the energy and the determination for great accomplishment. Our economic situation at home and our trading relations abroad are under continuous and expert vigilance.
To those Canadian firms and salesmen who have demonstrated their competitive ability in foreign markets and who have co-operated so fully with us, I extend my thanks and my congratulations. I urge them to keep up the good work and to exert their influence on their less progressive fellows. To the men and

women of the department, I offer my appreciation for their devotion and for a job well done. To all Canadians who require help or guidance in the commercial field, I hold out an invitation. The Department of Trade and Commerce is at your service.

This table shows that in 1958 world exports amounted to $96,080 million. In 1959 they went up to $101,780 million, an increase of 5.9 per cent. During that same period Canada's exports went up by 4.9 per cent, so that we did not maintain our position; we fell behind the rate of growth in world exports during that period. If we take the period January to September, 1960, and I have figures for only that period, we find that world exports went up to $111,300 million U.S. dollars, an increase of 9.3 per cent, while
Canada's exports went up only 2.3 per cent. Therefore we are not holding our own in the world's markets because our increase in world trade want down from 4.9 per cent in 1959 to 2.3 per cent in the period up to September, 1960. When we compare the increase of 2.3 per cent in Canadian exports with the 9.3 per cent increase in world exports, we see that Canada is failing to keep pace with the increase in world trade.
The minister referred to the higher exports to our overseas markets, and it seems to me he was making a virtue of necessity because he failed to mention that the economies of

Supply-Trade and Commerce overseas markets are experiencing an unprecedented boom which puts them in a position to buy more goods and thus increase their imports. On the other hand, Canada has been experiencing a kind of recession, and this puts us in an unfavourable position as far as imports are concerned. I do not think it is far fetched to allege that these two factors are in some way related to what appeared to be an overly bright picture of Canada's performance in the world export market and the improvement so far as Canadian imports are concerned.
Therefore my first criticism of the minister's statement is that it did not give us the complete picture. I think at a time like this we must be honest with ourselves and with the Canadian people and not try to create an impression of optimism and wellbeing that may not be completely justified by the facts.
My second criticism of the minister's statement is that he said nothing at all about the deficit in what we call invisible exports, and that is the major part of our overseas trade deficit problem. I would be one of the first to admit that items such as interest, dividends and insurance possibly come within the realm of fiscal policy, but they also affect the minister's department and he must work out his policies in conjunction with those of his colleagues and try to do something about this problem of the invisible exports.
There is one matter about which I think a great deal could be done, and that is the imbalance on our tourist trade. I do not have the exact figures, but I think last year that imbalance amounted to about a quarter of a billion dollars. Although it does involve the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, yet here again is a matter for collaboration among the minister and his colleagues to try to work out some solution to this problem. A more vigorous sales promotion of the goods we produce has, according to the minister, produced favourable results, and surely it is not outside our capacity or ingenuity to devise some method of promoting and increasing our tourist trade.
The third criticism I have to offer is that the statement of policy given by the minister today did not indicate any appreciation of the kind of world we are living in and the forces which are influencing our relationships, and particularly our trade relationships, with other countries and are going to influence them a great deal more in the future. I think the minister caught the imagination of the Canadian people with his conference of trade commissioners, and also with his follow-up provincial conference for trade promotion. The minister brought his commissioners here, as well as businessmen. They pooled their ideas
fMr. Carter.]
and explored prospects. They got a pep talk from the minister, I am told, and were sent back to work harder and harder to promote sales. No one will deny that this in itself is good, but I think the question we must ask ourselves is whether it is sufficient.
It seems to me that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is somewhat in the position of a general. He has his intelligence service; he has his commissioners who are his reconnaissance troops; he has his captains of industry, and he has his little army of merchandisers. A good general not only has a good plan of action but also briefs his troops. As members of the house representing the people I think today the minister should have briefed us and the Canadian people generally more fully on the facts of life in the field of world trade.
What is Canada's position in a rapidly changing world? What are the forces influencing our trade efforts? What should be our plan of action taking all these factors into consideration? I think the first step that should be taken is self-examination. We profess to believe in a system of free enterprise and, in fact, we are not a state trading nation. Most of our deals with other countries are carried out between individuals. We have developed a system which has operated on the belief that out of the competitive efforts of individuals all striving to get the best for themselves will come the greatest efficiency; that the weak will go to the wall and the strongest and most efficient will survive, resulting in the greatest good for the greatest number.
There is no doubt that the free enterprise system we have built up has developed some great advantages. It has developed some good qualities in the individuals who are engaged in business; qualities of alertness, imagination, courage, endurance, initiative and responsibility, skill, flexibility and determination, and that is all to the good. It has also produced great material benefits in the form of inventions, manufacturing processes, jobs in the development of resources and the harnessing of power.
But we must not permit these advantages to blind us to any weaknesses that may be inherent in our system, and it cannot be denied that weaknesses do exist; because against the benefits I have mentioned we must set a list of less happy results. We know that good, sound businesses have sometimes been destroyed and that workers have been exploited. We have had walk-outs, strikes and the bitterness that results from them. We have sometimes had bad goods and sometimes when shortages were in sight we have had unwarranted stockpiling regardless of the needs of other people, with the result that production has slowed down elsewhere for lack of the materials lying unused in frozen stockpiles.

We hear sometimes of price conspiracies and conspiracies to restrict competition. We have had some examples of that in the electrical industries south of the border. There was also a report in the papers last night of something similar in the drug industry. In addition, sometimes the opposite occurs; surplus goods are flooded on the market regardless of the damage that may be done at home or abroad.
These weaknesses must be corrected if we are going to withstand the forces that we shall have to contend with in the future. I think they have developed mainly because we have had no goal outside of our own selfinterest. We have been engaged in developing what has been called the affluent society, and once we have created this affluent society we somehow bend our efforts mainly toward preserving it and increasing the affluence. In other words we become security minded, and we tend to lose the driving forces, the skill, determination and initiative that created this society in the first place.
I think the irony of this situation is that once a certain stage has been reached, free enterprise people themselves clamour for government interference which in the end must destroy some of their liberties. Every time the government passes a law some individual liberty or freedom is interfered with.
For a general to encourage his troops to go out and work harder doing the same things may not help to solve our problem. I think the minister is to be commended for the emphasis he has placed on taking responsibilities. If I have read the reports of his activities correctly, I take it that he has encouraged individual businessmen to assume more responsibility for the nation and for the welfare of our economy. But I think we must go beyond that, because what we do will be determined by the goals we have in mind. We need new goals now, new motives and a new direction, because the affluent society as an end in itself does not satisfy human aspirations and the longing in human hearts. The individual businessman must have a broader and more far-reaching aim than simply running a smoothly operating enterprise purely for the purpose of making a profit or getting ahead of his competitors. If he continues to be dominated by these motives he will in the end be destroyed. We must have new, specific and overriding purposes which will govern our policies and our practices.
Yesterday our leader set forth some of these goals. The Liberal party has always stood for the freest trade possible consistent with our national security. This, he pointed out, is to be achieved not overnight but under a long,
28. 1961
Supply-Trade and Commerce well planned program, step by step. He suggested, as a first step, that we try to work toward an Atlantic trading community.
That point was very well developed yesterday and other speakers will be developing it still further today, so I shall pass on to another point which I think should have been included in the minister's statement. The minister gave no indication today that our national security and survival depend practically as much on his department as on the Department of National Defence. We cannot separate our security from our trading activities. I feel it would have been wise if today the minister had given a much fuller outline of the forces that are at work in this part of the field of world trade.
He mentioned the emergence of trading blocs, the inner six and the outer seven, and this situation, too, will be further developed by other speakers from our party. However, he did not mention the fact that trading and industry today are a battleground in the struggle for world domination. If we are going to develop a plan we must take that into consideration. The minister did not make any reference to it at all.
We have had some very stirring examples of what is happening in this economic battleground. Russia has developed a well thought out and well integrated program which contains four points. The first point is an intensive industrial expansion inside the Soviet bloc itself. A measure of that expansion can be seen when we realize that in 1927 Russia produced only 3 per cent of world production, whereas in 1955 she produced 20 per cent and doubtless today it is much higher than that.
The second point in that program is industrial sabotage in the industrialized countries of the west. We have seen some examples of that. The third point is a selective disruption of normal trading relations of the free world. We have had examples of that, the tendency of the Soviet union to weld its satellites into an economic bloc with an economy complementary to its own.
Perhaps I might just mention one example. In 1957 there was a world surplus of tin. Russia is a great importer of tin and buys a great deal of it from red China. When we have a situation in which there is a surplus of a product, as there was with tin, we would normally expect a country to buy that product. What did Russia do? Instead of buying and stockpiling tin at that time, Russia sold between 10,000 and 11,000 tons of tin at a price lower than the world market. By so doing Russia disrupted the economies of Bolivia, Malaya and Nigeria,

Supply-Trade and Commerce as well as other countries. This is the sort of thing we must expect on a much more intensive scale in the future.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, if we are going to successfully meet that kind of challenge we must develop a well co-ordinated plan. I think the first part of that plan should be concentration on building up trade with countries whose economies are complementary to our own. We have certain economies very close to us. We have the West Indies Federation, and it was a great disappointment to me that the minister did not even mention that country during his presentation today.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if I might call it one o'clock.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this morning the minister outlined certain actions which his department had taken to improve our world trade position. In reply I pointed out the fact that trade and industry are now a battleground in the struggle for world domination and that further action was essential based on that consideration. In order to be successful such action must have a global purpose, a global strategy and involve total commitment.
As a first step I suggested that, without diminishing our efforts elsewhere, we should place special emphasis on developing economic ties with those countries whose economies were complementary to our own. I then cited the British West Indies Federation as an example and expressed disappointment that in his presentation the minister had made no mention of trade possibilities with these countries.
The British West Indies Federation and the Caribbean area have been a market for salt cod for over 200 years and for that reason are of special interest to the Atlantic provinces, and in particular to my own province of Newfoundland. I am informed that this market has seriously deteriorated during recent months owing for the most part to the

inability of Cuba to purchase our salted fish products. In this connection I call to the minister's attention the fact that one of the most glaring omissions in his presentation this morning was his failure to give the committee a progress report on our trade relations with Cuba. While I am on the subject of omissions, may I also mention his failure to make any reference to uranium contracts. I do not intend to take the time of the committee to dwell on these subjects because they will be dealt with by my colleagues.
To come back to the subject of fish markets in the British West Indies and in the Caribbean area, I remind the minister that fish exporters now claim that the abolition of NAFEL has handicapped their marketing efforts. I have never held any particular brief for NAFEL. It had many features which did not appeal to me personally. Nevertheless it had a purpose to fulfil. If it had not had a purpose to fulfil, it would never have been created. It now seems that the mistake has been not so much the abolition of NAFEL as the failure to put any other organization in its place.
Before I leave the subject of the British West Indies may I remind the minister also that the selling of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships fleet now also seems to have been a mistake. These ships were not costing Canada very much. The continuance of the link they provided between the British West Indies and Canada, at a time when these countries are coming together in a political federation and are trying to integrate their economies, would have well repaid the small deficits the country incurred on their behalf.
As a second step in this plan of action I suggest that some means should be developed in order to protect Canada from economic aggression and penetration. Also, on the world scale, there is a need for a body to be organized as a sort of counterpart of NATO in the economic field in order to help countries resist economic penetration and to offset any efforts that might be made to disrupt their economies such as those I mentioned this morning with reference to the Soviet purchase and disposal of tin when there was a world surplus.
Lest my C.C.F. friends misunderstand what I am proposing I should like to make it clear that I am not advocating state planning. What I am suggesting is voluntary planning by free people within the country and under government leadership and direction and, among the nations of the world, voluntary association on the part of free nations which have come together to plan with a common goal and a common purpose.

This will no doubt involve some painful decisions on the part of different industries, different sectors of the economies of the countries involved and on the part of individual countries in their relations with one another. However, on our capacity to rise above self-interest and accept this challenge may depend our survival as free men and free nations.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to this House of Commons and to the people in general all departments of government are important, but I do not think I will be challenged when I say that in my estimation one of the most important departments of government is that the estimates of which are now before us, the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Canada is rather unique in the world. She is a country which is, I believe, almost 4,000 miles in breadth, extends from the joint U.S.-Canadian border up to the Arctic circle, is one of the wealthiest countries in the world in natural resources, is one third larger in territory than the United States, has a population of 18 million, and whose maintaining the second highest standard of living in the world is dependent upon the fact that we are an export nation.
That is why I say that the estimates we have before us now are from a department of the utmost importance. We listened this morning to a quite comprehensive statement by the minister. He undoubtedly gave us some interesting information and statistics. I must say that in my opinion a general analysis of the statement given by the minister is that it was tempered in a manner which gave a rosy hue to the export-import picture as far as our country is concerned. Because of that I must admit I was a little disappointed in the approach of the minister.
Over the years I have often heard it said that the difference between a statesman and a politician is that a statesman has read a book. I do not agree with that interpretation. I think the right definition is that a statesman says what has to be said, whereas a politician says that which he thinks will meet with the approval of his party and the people.
There are times when a tough decision has to be made. I am afraid the minister did not make that decision in his remarks this morning. He presented rather, a picture of the past and statistics, instead of what is now required from a statesman, an analysis of our present situation.
We should have been given an analysis of the possibilities, potentialities, problems and dangers of the future and how Canada, as an export nation, is going to face up to those problems, potentialities and, I am going to say, dangers.
28, 1961
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I admit that the minister did mention some of these things, but I think the emphasis was on the wrong place. Naturally we are all very happy to receive any and all reports from the minister as to any progress that has been made, or any change that has been made to bring our trade into balance as between exports and imports.
However, I do feel it is imperative that we have on the part of the minister and the government, of which the hon. gentleman is a distinguished member, a recognition of the difficulties which we face. The statistics, as rosy as he can make them, do not take care of the 700,000 or 800,000 unemployed persons in Canada. Because of the situation in our Canadian economy, with that number of unemployed, statistics are not enough. We need an enunciation of policies that will put every Canadian to work. Canada is an export nation, and we need at least an outline as to the real and serious danger that we face today, or we will face tomorrow, because of the growing number of economic trading blocs, the inner six and the outer seven, and because of what must now be recognized in the economic cold war, which is not only being threatened by the Soviet bloc but of which we have already seen many instances in these past 18 months.
Therefore with that grave and serious responsibility, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to face not only the situation in Canada, with its present high unemployment, but the economic cold war, the establishment of trading blocs, and the increased efficiency and automation which is going on in other countries of the world with whom we have to compete. If Canada does not compete, our economy will come very close to collapse.
Interesting as the minister's remarks were, it was that kind of emphasis, that kind of truthfulness to the Canadian people that I hoped he would express when he opened vote No. 1 this morning.
We are facing difficult problems; there is no question about that. Nobody in Canada wants to see a reduction in our standard of living. Everybody wants to see full employment. I am afraid that very often we members of the House of Commons-I include all hon. members-are not honest enough with the Canadian people in giving them the true picture that we, as an export nation, face in world affairs today.
I feel this is a responsibility that many of us do not accept to the degree and depth that we should, because unfortunately too many of us are more interested in saying things which we consider necessary.
With the establishment of the trading blocs, and perhaps more to come, the recovery of the nations of the world from the impact

Supply-Trade and Commerce and holocaust of the last world war, the efficiency and automation that is going on at a more rapid pace outside Canada than it is here, there has to be a recognition that we can only maintain our status and standards by an understanding among government, management and labour. We must produce goods of quality and in a quantity to supply our consumption needs. If we fail to meet competition from abroad because of poor production efficiency and lack of co-operation by all sectors of our industry the consequences will be serious to all concerned.
As I have already said, I think that in view of the world situation in trade and commerce an increased investment in the services of the trade commissioners of the department is imperative. I heard with great regret only the other day some of the most experienced and efficient trade commissioners in the department have either left or are leaving the service at the very time when we are in greatest need of their knowledge, experience and brains. Because of their experience and their contacts they are being bought up by free enterprise in Canada, the offers made being so fantastic that despite the loyalty of these men and their love of the service they cannot reject them. I am very sorry to hear this, because if ever there was a time when we need the services of these men it is right now and in the days and years that lie ahead.
I sincerely hope the Minister of Finance is not being penny wise and pound foolish; I hope a policy of that kind has not been responsible for what occurred. Private industry may need these trained men but Canada needs them even more in these days of competition. I know the government cannot match some of the offers which have been made by free enterprise, but something more could surely be done. In the last two years it has been my privilege to meet a good many of these trade commissioners in their posts throughout the world. I think I know of their love of the service and their loyalty to it, and I have no hesitation in saying that money spent to hold these men in the service of Canada is money well spent and its provision would be supported, I am sure, by the Canadian people if the picture were made clear to them.
A few years ago when I was in provincial politics and came within one elected member of being a premier, somebody said to me "You are an electrician. What are you going to do?" I said "Hire the brains and pay for them." I think that is a good practice in government as well as in free enterprise. As I say, we have serious problems before us. We shall require clear headed and sensible thinking if we are to face up to what is developing

throughout the world in the export field. The government, as well as all hon. members of this committee, will realize the complexities of this problem. They will realize that as individuals, or as groups of individuals in industry, we cannot put selfish interest before the good of Canada as a whole. This is definitely one of the problems involved in government policy inasmuch as we want protectionism at home sometimes in relation to certain industries while failing to recognize that since our economy is mainly based on export we cannot export unless we import. If we are going to be paid for export in Canadian dollars we have to import, too, whether we like it or not, rough as that may be. I have no hesitation in saying that we are not explaining this sufficiently to the Canadian people so that they may realize that individual or partisan interests must depend upon policies designed for the benefit of Canada as a whole. I have said this outside the house and I have no hesitation in saying it here.
I have until this moment been speaking in generalities, but, I hope it will be recognized sincerely and on broad principles. Much more has got to be done in the future, even if it is admitted that everything possible has been done in the past by the minister and by the Department of Trade and Commerce. We must intensify our work and effort. We must not only draw attention to those things which are rosy; we must also point out the difficulties and shortcomings which are of a serious nature and try to figure out how to correct the situation. Perhaps we have failed in the past. Let us, then, do something different in the future.
I understand that over the last four months the minister has received a somewhat voluminous correspondence from British Columbia, from a firm which has been and which still is, I think, one of the major exporters of timber from my province. I, also, have received correspondence. It disturbed me and intrigued me so much that when I was last in Vancouver I made an appointment to see the president and the executive officers of this company, and asked them to produce the material in front of me. I regret I have not had the opportunity of checking completely the information given me, but the minister can challenge it if he has found it to be incorrect.
Accepting the statistics which have been provided me, it would appear that until about five years ago Canada used to enjoy about a 50 per cent share in the sawn lumber, logs, poles and pilings imported into Japan from North America. However, the figures for exports of these materials in the five years ending in 1960 show a different picture. Of sawn lumber entering Japan from North

America 11.9 per cent came from Canada and 88.91 per cent from the United States. Log exports from Canada dropped to 3.12 per cent compared with 96.8 per cent in the United States. Poles and pilings dropped to 10.51 per cent from Canada and 89.49 per cent from the United States. Information which I received in Vancouver indicated that in the first 10 months of 1960 sawn lumber exports from British Columbia to Japan were only 3.53 per cent of the exports from British Columbia and the United States Pacific states; that our exports of logs had dropped to 1.92 per cent. Our poles and pilings stayed fairly stable; they dropped from 10.51 per cent to 9.98 per cent.
I wish to make one point unmistakably clear. I am fully in support of the principle that Canada and British Columbia with their vast resources, should not have an economy in which we are hewers of wood and drawers of water. To the absolute extent possible we should process our own natural resources and not export our raw material. But, in the processing of our raw material, the timber of British Columbia, what has happened? If the information I have from this major exporter in British Columbia is correct, our sawn lumber exports to Japan which used to be 50 per cent, on a five-year average had dropped to 11.09 per cent and in the first 10 months of 1960, they were down to 3.53 per cent. I am certain that with the resources in timber which we have in British Columbia and the efficiency of our logging industry, we should be able to compete, but we have lost out.
Of course, it is important to know why we lost out, but what is more important is can we regain the market? I hope the minister will comment on this. However, there is also another point that I wish to raise, but in doing so I do not want to be misunderstood. If we can process our raw materials in Canada, let us do so. We must process. Secondary industry is a must. A manufactured product means a lot more to the economy of Canada and the standard of living of our people than exporting the raw goods and importing manufactured goods. But if there is a time when we cannot process the raw material and we cannot export and therefore the logs, let us say, are going to go to waste, then there is something wrong.
In those circumstances if because of provincial and federal responsibility a situation arises under which we would rather have the teredos eat up the logs in the water than export the logs, then there is something wrong. From the talk I had with the executive officials in Vancouver and from the large amount of correspondence I have had with different people concerned it is my understanding that because of certain regulations
Supply-Trade and Commerce we would prefer to see the teredos attack the logs in the water than accept contracts from countries which would like to buy the logs. I am not speaking of our major timber, I am speaking of what is known in the terminology of the trade as short ends. I think my hon. friend from Kootenay West will tell me if I am wrong.
By reason of the provincial and federal responsibility we have this situation. There may be short end logs in the water. If a buyer in Japan, for example, should write to an exporting broker and ask him to fill an order he would be told that he cannot answer. Why can he not answer? He cannot answer because the regulation says that in order to get an export permit the logs must be in the water for no fewer than 60 days. There must have been a scaling 30 days before the expiration of the 60 days, and the logs must be offered to saw mills or pulp mills for purchase. Then, at the end of the 60 days and the 30 days scaling and two companies, the saw mills or the pulp mills, have rejected the offer to buy the short end logs for processing in British Columbia, they can then apply for an export permit.
