speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question for clarification? To my mind it is a provincial regulation. Is it in fact a provincial regulation that demands this?

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
There is a combination of the two. I have in front of me information having to do with the federal regulations. What I have just said applies to the federal regulation, but there is a combination of the two, and I tried to make that clear. That is why I think there has to be understanding and cooperation. But here is the point. When I was at the meeting of those forestry executives in Vancouver there were two offers which came from Japan that morning to buy millions of board-feet of those short end logs. I said to the president of that company, "What are you going to do with it?" He said, "I am going to turn them down." I said, "Why; are the logs not available?" He said, "There are whole booms of logs within three miles of where you are sitting. I cannot get them because they have to be 60 days in the water and scaled, and then I have to go to the saw mill companies and the pulp companies and get one of them interested enough to come down and say 'We will not buy'."
Under the circumstances this would mean work for the loggers of British Columbia. Those are logs which are going to be attacked by teredos; they will be attacked by teredos because that is the situation. I think this is a very serious situation. But the province of British Columbia does not want any change. In principle I can understand why. Let us

Supply-Trade and Commerce process in our pulp mills and saw mills in British Columbia. But, Mr. Chairman, I ask this question and I hope the minister will comment on it. These logs are going to be attacked by toredos and once they are attacked by teredos they are no good for pulp and no good for saw mills. Why do we have to waste that natural resource; why do we have to leave these short ends on the ground or in the water, if nobody will process them in British Columbia or in Canada? Why do we have to say, "Let this natural resource rot" rather than get some return for it?
I hope this is understood by all hon. members. I repeat it the third time. I want the material to be processed in Canada. In circumstances such as these it would mean very much to our young men and much more to the British Columbia economy. Why do we have to retain provincially or federally this kind of regulation? Could something not be worked out to protect the processing in British Columbia and protect secondary industry also in that province?
With respect to the short ends left in the water or on the land when the good stuff is taken out, can a plan not be evolved whereby Canada will get a return from the export of these short ends instead of their being left for food for the teredos? There are some here who are well acquainted with the timber industry of British Columbia and they know how the teredos go to work on the logs in the booms in the ocean waters of British Columbia. I want to draw that particular point to the attention of the minister and ask for his comment thereon.
In particular, I want to draw to his attention the change not in the amount of our exports of sawn lumber, logs, poles and piling to Japan but rather the drop in the percentage we are able to export to that country compared with the amount exported by the United States. Something has gone wrong, and I draw this matter to the attention of the minister and ask that particular attention be paid to it.
In the matter of exports generally to the countries of the world, I feel quite certain that if the minister could have more men, retain his trained personnel and persuade the Minister of Finance that the expenditure of money to maintain and increase our exports is money well spent and directly or indirectly results in returns to our economy and the people of Canada, he would be able to bring about some improvement.
I conclude as I started by saying that I consider this department to be one of the most important departments of government and I hope the minister will be able to give us more information later as to how the

problem facing us in going to be attacked. We will give him every assistance we can but where required we will also criticize.

Mr. Chairman, I am not as well prepared at this time to speak on this important subject as I should like to be and my remarks will be directed primarily toward problems that affect the area in which I live. First of all, I should like to extend to the minister my sincere congratulations and those of the people of the riding I represent for the splendid effort he is making in building up Canada's export market and also preserving our home market. As I said, I intend to deal more or less with local matters. I might say that in the area from which I come we grow a very large proportion of the tender fruits and vegetables that are grown in Canada and we also have more than 200 diversified industries. When I review these industries it surprises me to note the number of different types of industries we have. Some of them depend almost entirely on the export market, and I am thinking particularly of the pulp and paper industries of which we have several. We also have some industries which depend on both the export market and our own market and we have a very large number of small industries that depend almost entirely on the Canadian market.
For these reasons it can be seen that in my riding we depend very much on a balanced economy. M^e cannot afford to have too much in the way of imports come into the country because it may ruin industries that depend on the home market and yet we must not set up road-blocks that will interfere with our export market.
It would sometimes seem that the Customs Tariff and the provision respecting value for duty are regarded as bad words in this house but nevertheless these are two very important pieces of legislation in controlling our trade and commerce and they must be brought up to date from time to time. In reviewing the problems of our local industries one is often very much convinced that there is reason for changes in these measures. I might cite one instance that came to my attention a few weeks ago in connection with a plant that was established in our area in 1955 and started production in 1957. Many millions of dollars are involved in the building and machinery and the development that took place in order to get the plant into production. The industry in question has been able to supply its product to the Canadian trade and has also done a considerable amount of export business. The company produces a type of specialized fire brick. A considerable

amount of reinforced steel is used in this production of the fire brick but the basic material required is magnesite ore.
I presume there is a lot of magnesite ore in Canada which may be suitable for this type of brick, but at the present time only two bodies of ore are in production and both are under the control of another company. The firm to which I refer is in the very unhappy and unfortunate position of having to pay a duty of 15 per cent on the raw material they bring into Canada while the finished fire brick is allowed to enter Canada duty free. There is a case where an industry is being penalized for being in business.
The point I should like to make is that there are many different items in our Customs Tariff that should be reviewed and changed. At the present time, unfortunately, practically all of these items are tied up under GATT and it is very difficult to get anything done. I might say that this industry flourished and did well. It supplied a very fine type of brick to such industries as the Steel Company of Canada, the Portland Cement Company and the International Nickel plants at Sudbury but today they find that a similar product is entering Canada from other countries duty free. This is affecting their sales and unless they receive some protection they are going to be out of business. I feel that trade and commerce is not only a matter of export but also a matter of our home market as well, and that is one of the problems I should like to place before the minister at this time.
There is also the question of value for duty purposes, something that is often debated in the house with some heat, but from my observations in connection with the values for duty on certain items coming into Canada I find that the values for duty on some goods are very unrealistic.
I might cite just one example, the matter of radio tubes. I mentioned this in the committee before, but I do not mind bringing it up again because I find the value for duty placed on these tubes coming in from a certain country is 29 and 31 cents whereas the value which has been arrived at in the country from which they come and used by the trade commissioner of that country is 60 cents. This represents a very unfair situation with which we in this country have to contend. I think that if our values for duty on imports from low wage countries were realistic, I do not mean the actual Canadian cost but the costs arrived at in the country in which they are made, we would find our imports from those countries would be very much higher than they are at the present time in dollar value.
This puts the Minister of Trade and Commerce at very great disadvantage. I hesitate
Supply-Trade and Commerce to mention Japanese products, but that is one country I have in mind. We are told all the time that Japan is buying much more from us than we are buying from them. However, if a realistic value for duty were established on the goods coming into this country from Japan, I am sure the tables would be turned and we would be buying much more in dollar value from Japan.
There is another matter about which I am deeply concerned and that is that many of our industries in the Niagara peninsula have reached a point in their production where they can compete with the United States. Now, that is quite a statement to make but I know it is a fact in some cases. Many of these industries have built up quite a business with the United States. There is one practice in which the United States indulges, although I do not know whether or not they do it intentionally, and that is the changing of tariff regulations practically overnight.
I could cite the experience of one firm in this connection. This firm received a substantial contract from the United States. The goods were manufactured and a substantial shipment made. The firm received another big contract. The goods were made ready for shipment but instead of being shipped via Niagara Falls as they had been before they were put across the border at Detroit. The American customs appraiser at that point held up the shipment. Apparently he is a power unto himself because he increased the tariff from something like 30 per cent to about 45 per cent and told the company that if they did not want to accept his ruling they would have to appeal to Washington. In the meantime, the goods were held up at the border for three weeks and demurrage was paid on them. The decision of the appraiser at Detroit was confirmed. As a result this firm lost money instead of making a few dollars. This is a condition about which perhaps we cannot do anything, but I think it is a condition that should never be forgotten when we are dealing with the United States in matters of trade and commerce.
I am sure many hon. members will recall that a short time ago, almost overnight, the United States raised its tariff on bicycles imported from Canada from something like 30 per cent up to 50 per cent. This had a very vital effect on the Canadian bicycle industry.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a problem that is developing in Canada today in connection with not only our coastal shipping but also our lake shipping. We all know that Great Britain built up a tremendous world trade through having ships to take the goods to their destination. The condition in Canada today is deteriorating. Living along the banks of the Welland

Supply-Trade and Commerce ship canal, as I do, I have noticed that the number of European ships going through the canal is increasing all the time. These ships are hauling freight at prices that Canadian ships cannot meet. I had the opportunity of visiting a British freighter last year, a 10,000 tonner, which was engaged in bringing cargo from South America. This vessel carried a crew of 40. There were five white officers and 35 Hindus who were paid $40 per month. They got their food and cooked it themselves. The agreement under which they were hired stipulated that they would sign up for three years and that they would be taken home at least once during those three years. This is a condition which we in Canada simply do not want to match.
We know that at the present time some Canadian vessels are being transferred to British registry, just as the Canada steamship lines are transferring some of their vessels to Bermuda registry. Scott Misener is considering action along the same lines. This type of thing could spread very rapidly and, in a short time, we could find we had very little in the way of Canadian shipping on our great lakes. This situation applies not only to lake vessels but also to vessels plying the St. Lawrence river and our coastal areas. I am greatly concerned about the transfer of these ships to foreign registry because I feel that should some world disturbance take place these foreign ships would be withdrawn from our service and we would not have any vessels with which to move our own goods. I feel this is a matter which the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take into consideration. If we are going to build ourselves up as a trading nation, then it seems to me imperative that we have a strong merchant fleet not only on the great lakes but also a fleet that would be capable of taking goods to practically all parts of the world. The situation is certainly not developing along those lines at the moment.
I have not got a great deal more to say, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to make some comment on a speech delivered by Mr. Coyne. If Mr. Coyne is on your side then he is your friend, but if he is against you then he is not. In this case, as always, I think his words are very true, and I should like to quote them:
We cannot expect to go on indefinitely buying goods and services from abroad in amounts greatly in excess of our exports, that is, buying on credit on a scale which requires large further increases in our foreign debt.
Then, he goes on to say that corrections must be made and he concluded by saying:
The sooner we can make substantial progress in this direction, the stronger and more secure will be our economic future and national integrity.


We all know that our imbalance of trade, while it may have improved somewhat, is a matter that gives us a great deal of concern. The other day I saw some figures, and I probably cannot quote them exactly, which indicated that Great Britain purchased goods abroad to the extent of something like $54 per person per year; Germany, something like $46; the United States, $19 per person per year, and Canada, the small country that we are, was purchasing abroad about $275 worth of goods per person per year. These are figures which stagger all of us because, after all is said and done, running a country is just like running a business or a household. If you spend more than you bring in you are soon going to go broke.
This concludes my remarks at this time, Mr. Chairman and I hope I have contributed something of value toward this debate.

Mr. Chairman, it is generally conceded that Canada is going through a difficult period, more fundamental than a mere period of business recession. Were it not for the unusually large number of unemployed, the situation would not be so serious. However, we are confronted with this problem in which no one finds satisfaction; and as we analyse the causes we cannot help but point the finger to, at least as a contributing factor, the inability to maintain Canadian exports at a level which would ensure increased growth in the economy.
I have had occasion to say it before and I repeat that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, notwithstanding his industrious application to the job, which is commendable, has not been able to shake off the shackles of a tariff policy, imposed upon his department, which is not conducive to improving our trading position with other nations. I do not propose to repeat what I said here last Tuesday on the subject of tariffs. I shall, however, endeavour to indicate to the minister some of the reasons why I think we are suffering from competition in the markets of the world, the effects of which are plainly visible in our unemployment picture.
The first reason which comes to my mind is the government's attitude toward United States capital. The sport of giving United States investments another punch in the nose seems to be in some quarters as popular as ever. Indeed, some speakers seem to be forever dedicated to fostering animosity towards anything American, whether it is newspapers, telecasts, radio programs or capital investment. They do this in the name of rugged "Canadianism", perhaps not realizing that by doing so they are actually hurting themselves.

The president of the Royal Bank of Canada in a speech he delivered early in the year warned the Canadian people against what he called "The almost hysterical wave of sentiment against the import of foreign capital". Mr. Chairman, we cannot hope to expand our export business unless we have first sufficient capital to develop our primary industries. A case in point is a recent statement made by Mr. M. S. Fotheringham, president of Steep Rock Iron Mines, to the effect that it might be impractical for his company to proceed with developments at Lake St. Joseph without extensive financial backing from United States firms. This is a company which has been responsible for the export to the United States of more than 25 million tons of iron ore. The cost of the development of the Steep Rock Iron Range Mines, including the Caland Company of Cleveland ore deposits leased to that company by Steep Rock Iron Mines Ltd., was well in excess of $100 million. These ore bodies are continuously being subjected to progressive exploration. This gigantic enterprise would not have been possible without ample capital. I scarcely need to add, Mr. Chairman, that this mining operation has meant millions of dollars to the credit side of our exports. Contrary to the opinion of some people that investments in our primary industries especially from the United States are merely exploiting and are interested only in the accumulation of profits, I wish to quote from the annual statement of the company which reveals the fact that this mining project since commencement in 1945 has netted a profit of $60 million from all of which there was reinvestment in expansion and development, giving employment to hundreds of millions and not one cent has yet been paid in dividends to its shareholders. I may add that Canada expects to be exporting some 80 million tons a year of iron ore by 1975 and about 100 million by 1990. This is a statement also made by the president of Steep Rock Iron Mines.
United States investment in Canada is the story of a great contribution to the development of Canada which was made in the first instance at the instigation of private industry as well as at the invitation of the Canadian government of the day which was chiefly responsible for the great manufacturing facilities which provide most of our exports, outside of grain such as pulp and paper, nickel, aluminum, automobiles and parts and other products. Only yesterday, an account appeared in the Montreal Gazette which reported a substantial sale of car radios to the United States by R.C.A. Victor Co. Ltd., the Canadian company, designed and developed here in Canada. Incidentally, I may say that

Supply-Trade and Commerce this company during the past three years has sold to the United States more than $4 million of technical equipment, and in competition with some of the largest manufacturers of electronic equipment in that country. It seems that this company policy of developing its own products has paid off and it should serve as an example to other manufacturers in adopting similar methods of enterprise.
Our economic ills have been dissected by several so-called experts. One of them, the governor of the Bank of Canada, made numerous pronouncements on the economic state of the nation. He has chosen several vehicles to launch his views. The latest was his appearance before the Senate manpower committee. According to reports, here again he was voicing the opinion that the Canadian people were living beyond their means. He pointed out that consumer debt of the Canadian public, once well below that of the United States in terms of personal income, was now almost at the same level. If he had said that we are living beyond our means in the sense that we are importing more goods in terms of dollars and cents than we are exporting, I would go along with him. But I am not of the belief that we are living beyond our means when we spend our money on goods manufactured here in Canada.
What created the prosperity and high standard of living which those of us who are employed are privileged to enjoy, is made possible precisely by the spending of the people in purchasing automobiles, appliances, better housing accommodation, clothing, furniture and a host of other commodities. Our banks and finance companies, in the majority of cases, provided the credit to finance these purchases which in turn created prosperity and not depression.
Contrary to the old fashioned thinking of putting your pennies into a sock and burying it for a rainy day, I believe that employment and a higher standard of living can be achieved in direct proportion to the velocity or speed of circulation which our currency attains and the revolving of credit.
The No. 1 objective-and I am sure it is the aim of the minister-is to trade with every country willing to trade with us on a reciprocal basis and remove the obstacles of unfair tariffs with nations who are buying more from us than we are buying from them.
While speaking on the amendment to the supply motion last Tuesday evening I gave credit to the minister for the trade commissioners' conference which he promoted last January. By way of suggestion I wish to bring to his attention that the department of commerce of the United States have

Supply-Trade and Commerce arranged for exporters to explain to small businessmen and manufacturers how to break into the export market.
The exporters will explain to these groups how it might benefit them to work together. They will also offer to act as consultants and brokers, cutting through red tape and making contact with buyers.
The department of commerce of the United States has also quietly lifted a 20-year old ban on publication of who receives export licences for the shipment of critical materials to foreign nations. Exporters encouraged continuation of the practice, which dates from world war II, because I presume they did not want competitors to know who their foreign customers were. Here, perhaps, is something our own government should look into and cut all the possible barriers to markets abroad.
However, the problem of export trade cannot be solved by any single remedy. There are many sides to the question and these should be examined. I propose to suggest ways which may be found worthy of consideration by the government.
Let us take a look at what is happening in some of the major trading nations of the world. Let us first take Japan as an example. We think of Japan as a country of 90 million people all busy making cheap goods to dump on world markets. It is a comparatively small country with a very small agricultural area. The Japanese cultivate every inch of it that will grow anything; but the area is pitifully small to feed 90 million people.
Japan must therefore import 40 per cent of her food or her people will starve. To make matters worse, she lacks raw materials. She imports iron ore, nickel, chromium and copper from Canada for her industries, and wheat for the major part of her food.
Japan must pay Canadian currency for the wheat and raw materials she imports from Canada. To earn Canadian dollars she must sell something to Canada. Without natural resources she can sell only the products of her factories. In other words, there has to be a two-way trade in order that other nations may do business with us.
The objection to this is that we import things that could be manufactured here. But can we not benefit more by selling that which we can produce better, and in abundance, in exchange for things which Japan may be better equipped to provide our markets?
We can honestly say competition for Canadian manufactured goods has been brought about not by the wish of the Japanese but by the sheer necessity of their so doing, or starving.

Mr. Chairman, during the last ACFAS convention held at the University of Montreal, a resolution was passed unanimously asking the federal government to establish a committee formed of experts in various fields-science, trade, engineering, administration-which would consider the methods of gradually introducing the metric system in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, these past few years the metric system has been used increasingly in Canada, more especially in the scientific field. It is known, for instance, that the Department of Fisheries, in its work, as well as in its publication, The Journal of the Fisheries Research of Canada, has been using this system of measurement exclusively. Moreover, at the outset of the work on the continental shelf project it was decided to use only the metric system. Finally, since the beginning of 1960, two of the most important geographical Canadian magazines, La Revue Canadienne de geographie and Les Cahiers de geographie de Quebec have decided to use the metric system on an exclusive basis. In the geo-90205-6-260
Supply-Trade and Commerce graphical branch itself, although the metric system is not used as a matter of course by all geographers, it is nevertheless used by those who co-operate in the continental shelf project.
On January 1st last, England and all the overseas territories coming under its jurisdiction adopted the centigrade degrees to measure temperature. This change applies not only to the scientific field but also to everyday life. In other terms, since the first of January last, English newspapers, radio and television stations have been giving their weather forecasts in centigrade units, according to the metric system.
It must be noted that this change is a first step toward the generalization of the metric system in all the spheres of everyday life in England. As a matter of fact, the adoption of the metric system was recommended in England in May 1960, following an extensive survey in the course of which a very large majority of personalities and qualified organizations took position in favour of the metric system.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to mention a few disadvantages due to the fact that our country has not yet adopted this metric system.
When tenders were called for the purchase of equipment required by a Middle East country, the Canadian bid was the lowest. However, it was not accepted.
The reason given the Canadian representative was the following:
Your equipment is very good and it can manufacture products that meet the requirements of the metric system, which is the one used in this country. But the trouble is that parts are machined according to your system of measurement. When the time comes for replacing those parts, this fact may mean expensive delays for us. Sorry.
The contract was therefore given to a German firm. Its bid was higher, but it was using the metric system for manufacturing parts. Those parts are available throughout the Middle East.
Mr. Chairman, these facts were reported in the December issue of the newspaper Perspectives.
A prominent Argentine manufacturer who came here on business spent hours consulting a Toronto firm's catalogue. The sales manager did not fail of course to point out to him machines which were lower priced than those offered by competing European companies. The South American scribbled figures over several sheets of paper and then closed the catalogue, took his hat and said:
Your prices may be more attractive, but I am so confused by your measures that I would rather pay more to European suppliers. They have the same measures as we have. What I would save
4118	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce on the purchase price would be more than erased by the loss of time and the unavoidable mistakes in converting yards into meters and gallons into litres.
Such incidents illustrate a harsh fact: our foreign trade will probably be conditioned by our system of measures. Throughout the world, Canadian products must compete with those of foreign manufacturers who have a great advantage in that their weights and measures are easily understood by customers, whereas ours are above the understanding of most of prospective purchasers.
Since our standard of living is closely related to world trade, all Canadians are affected by this confusion about measures. Furthermore, our unpractical system only makes things more complicated for everyone, mother and student, artist and engineer, scientist and farmer.
At present the standards of measure divide the world in two blocs. The commonwealth and the United States have the British system while the metric system is used in most of the rest of the world, namely Europe, U.S.S.R., red China, Japan, South America, Central America and the new African states. That means that 90 per cent of the world population enjoy the advantages of the metric system.
On our side, we are beginning to fear for the future of our exports. Yet, sentimental attachment to a traditional system may soon be upset by the necessities brought about by economic pressures.
India adopts the metric system. Eager to industrialize, India has bought just about everywhere the things that she needed. Will she now continue to import machines that will create nothing but confusion? Would Canadians buy lathes or tools of metric standards for their plants?
Again, I have quoted from the last December issue of Perspectives.
A parliamentary committee in New Zealand has recommended the adoption of the decimal system for money, to be followed by the adoption of the metric system. South Africa started on February 14 to convert her monetary system.
In the United Kingdom, a parliamentary committee has already recommended a total revision, and conversion of the monetary system has been advocated in a report prepared by several committees representing the British chambers of commerce association and the British association for the advancement of science. More than 2,000 organizations have submitted evidence and ideas.
It seems that the English monetary sys-


tem of pounds, shillings and pence, which has tormented generations of English students and innumerable tourists, is bound to disappear.
Another significant fact is that, according to the report, the metric weight and measures system will finally have to be adopted, but the report does not recommend that it should be made mandatory at once.
I would mention at this point, Mr. Chairman, that in the Department of National Defence, the metric system is fully accepted, particularly in the department's relations with our European partners in NATO.
The difficulties arising from different systems can be many and unfortunate. As an example, Bailey bridge sections made in the United States and in Great Britain could not be fitted together because the measurements were different.
Some Canadian businessmen see the situation realistically, but they are a minority.
The Canadian association of drug manufacturers made the change-over a few years ago and is now very happy about it. Measurements in electronics and photography are based on the metric system. Many of the firms involved have in fact found that the changeover had been less costly than anticipated.
Conversion on a national scale will probably depend to a large extent on the passing of a similar measure in the United Kingdom or the United States, but that is no excuse for inaction.
It is important, however, that eventually a committee be set up to consider the adoption of the metric system in Canada.
If a Canadian exporter finds he would stand to gain from the metric system, he should convert to it immediately.
Before applying the metric system across the country, we would have to have the answers to various questions. Should we act in conjunction with the United Kingdom and the United States? Should we apply a crash program or a long term one?
Some U.S. experts estimate that it will take 30 years to carry out conversion, in view of the high degree of that country's industrialization. The Indian plan provides for a 10-to 15-year period; the Japanese plan has a much shorter term. The South Africans expect it will take 18 months only to change their monetary system. A study of the metric system should be compulsory teaching in the schools. Of course, this point comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
We could also indicate the weight or volume of some products, such as groceries, in grains or litres; we might replace miles by kilometres on road maps and road signs. The biggest problem and the longest to solve will be the

conversion of machine tools, dies and gauges. Both systems would be used concurrently for a few years, while obsolete machines were being progressively replaced.
It would thus be possible to carry out conversion in 10 to 15 years. What is most important is that the organizations primarily concerned, such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Engineering Institute, immediately start tackling the problem.
At a time when the Soviet threat to our foreign trade is a cause for concern, it should be remembered that Russia holds a tremendous advantage in the metric system. The customer always prefers the easiest alternatives.
Our scientists use metric measurements, while our engineers measure things in inches, pounds and gallons. They waste precious time converting figures in either direction to co-ordinate their work.
We can well wonder to what extent the Russian advance in the field of space research may be attributed to closer co-operation between its engineers and scientists, all of whom use the metric system.
If we do not adopt the metric system, we run the risk of incurring enormous economic losses.
A moment ago, I gave a few examples in that connection. Some day, Canada will adopt the metric system and, Mr. Chairman, we must prepare for it now.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal briefly with two matters. First of all, about unemployment statistics, and then about our trade policy.
Mr. Chairman, item 399 of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce includes an amount for the dominion bureau of statistics. For some time, I have wanted to raise that matter. As I represent a typical working-class riding, I submit that the unemployment figures provided by the dominion bureau of statistics give us an incomplete picture of the situation. In my opinion, if we want to solve that problem, we must first of all realize its scope.
That is why it is important that the dominion bureau of statistics, on the basis of new standards, should submit each month on the basis new standards, figures that accurately reflect the gravity and scope of the unemployment problem.
90205-6-260i
Supply-Trade and Commerce
On April 15 or 16, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) told us that, according to the D.B.S. figures, there were, in Canada, 714,000 unemployed at the end of March. Now, as everyone knows, those figures are the result of very incomplete sampling. Perhaps they give us a picture of the situation, but I fear it is a rather sketchy picture.
A few days later, I asked the Minister of Labour how many Canadian citizens were drawing unemployment insurance benefits from our offices, at the end of March. He replied that on that date the number was 837,961.
Now, it is quite obvious that the unemployed, the man who draws unemployment insurance benefits, is unemployed within the meaning of the unemployment insurance act, because he has to submit evidence that he used to have a job, that he no longer has one for reasons beyond his control, that he has the required quantity of unemployment insurance stamps, and that he is available for work.
Now, how is it that, at the end of March, 837,961 persons were drawing benefits, while the figure given us by the D.B.S. is only 714,000?
This proves, therefore, that the D.B.S. figures are incomplete and do not show the extent of the problem.
Besides, there are millions of Canadian citizens who are out of work and who do not draw any unemployment insurance benefits.
If the minister, anxious to set up an adequate statistical system, would only refer this matter to the industrial relations committee, I would be in a position to prove that the number of unemployed who do not draw any benefits is about one third the number of those who do. At any time with the help of a few witnesses, I would be in a position to prove that.
Mr. Chairman, if we add the number of those who draw those benefits to the corresponding third of that number, we get a total of 1,110,114 unemployed. The purpose of my remarks with regard to the D.B.S. is to establish that, if we all want to solve this problem, we will have to change the standards for those statistics, because we have to know how many unemployed there are.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that this is the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), and not, of D.B.S. officials, even if they are experts in the

Supply-Trade and Commerce matter. If the minister did set up an adequate accounting system-and we have the necessary organization to do so-we might obtain every month figures which would prove that the situation is much worse than shown in present D.B.S. figures.
Again, I think that we, in this house, who are looking for an answer to the problem, should have more adequate figures. I therefore ask the minister to pay particular attention to my request, because I propose to raise the matter at every opportunity.
Mr. Chairman, I now want to say a few words about our policy in trade matters.
If I understood the minister well this morning, when he dealt with the matter his statement was read rather rapidly, but I jotted down as much as possible of the following remarks-he said:
We are trying to protect Canadian industry against the excessive risks of importations.
Now it is regrettable that we should have to recognize that results did not fulfil the government's hopes.
It is all right to wish and to express pious hopes, but this morning we expected a quite definite policy with regard to trade to be worked out.
In order to make it quite clear that our Canadian industries, in some sectors, are in an intolerable position, just because of imports, I would like to read a paragraph from an item published yesterday on the financial page of La Presse, and signed by Mr. Eugene Lafond, who said:
The flooding of the Canadian market by imported textiles now seems to be beyond all control. In fact the Canadian Apparel and Textile Manufacturers' Association reports that shipments of clothing and textiles from Hong Kong to Canada have increased by 38.6 per cent last year, and have now reached a value of $8.3 million, whereas it was $6 million in 1959, and $3 million in 1958.
For a number of years, the Canadian market was submerged by imports of Japanese textiles. Since Hong Kong textiles have appeared on our market, the latter is literally flooded; the situation has become unbearable, and when looking at the figures quoted by the association we find that, in 1960 alone, Hong Kong shipped to Canada 1,071,600 blouses, 2,366,364 shirts, 3,993,396 pairs of trousers and popular clothes of that kind, as well as 4,938,804 other pieces of woven clothing.
It has often been said that if the Canadian industry is unable to meet this competition, it is due to the extremely low level of salaries paid in the countries of Asia.
It is noted by the association that textiles sold in Hong Kong by Canada are not competing with the local product since ours are only partly finished goods which are finished, then re-exported;

this is not at all like the situation which prevails on the Canadian market.
Now, Mr. Chairman, our position is quite clear concerning Canada's trade policy. It was set forth unequivocally during the debate held this week, when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and other opposition members dealt with this matter. We are advocating the establishment of an economic community of Atlantic countries which, in my opinion, is one of the schemes likely to promote the development of Canadian trade.
Here is what I find in yesterday's issue of La Presse, in an editorial dealing with this debate and this matter:
What will Canada do when Great Britain, as she now seems resolved to do, decides to join the six of the common market, thereby granting preferred treatment to the products of those countries and putting our exports in the British Isles at a competitive disadvantage. We must ask ourselves whether, under the circumstances, the Canadian government should not consider right now modifying its trade policy to ward off the blow.
Canada has done nothing so far, nothing tangible at least, to protect our trade interests.
It must be recognized that, so far in the debate on this subject in the house, the position of the government has been purely negative.
Would it not be possible for our country to take part one way or another in the regrouping arrangement thought up by the European countries. It is the solution that was put forward by the opposition when it suggested the setting up of an Atlantic economic community as a complement to the defence community based on the North Atlantic treaty.
Mr. Chairman, those are the only remarks I wanted to make at this time. I will surely have questions to put when the different items of the department estimates are being looked into. Right now I should like to say to the minister that I am looking forward to the information he will give us in connection with vote 399. This vote has to do with unemployment statistics which, as I have said before, do not give a true picture of the seriousness and extent of this problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to be quite brief as usual and normal. First of all, I want to express my appreciation of the minister's courtesy and his very prompt attention to any matter I have brought to his attention. The same thing applies to his parliamentary secretary. I give them top marks as far as industry and courtesy are concerned, and I am sure all members appreciate that. I also want to express my appreciation of the work of the staff. A number

of times I have had occasion to make inquiries and I have always found my letters and all my inquiries replied to promptly and the information given as fully as possible.
While I listened with interest to the minister's review of the activities of his department, like former speakers I believe he failed to emphasize to some extent the difficulties that Canada is facing at the present time with respect to overseas trade particularly and the possible intensification of these difficulties in the months and years ahead. I refer to the difficulties which are caused by the formation of trading blocs, by the groups of countries that indulge in state trading, various pricing policies and the lowering of costs made possible through efficient arrangements as the result of co-operation, co-ordination and planning within the country or between certain countries.
The department's report this year is most attractive in format and very informative. I think there has been a great improvement in recent years in the reports put out by various departments. This is the second one within recent days that has shown great improvement over previous years. It is a credit to the printers, the persons who design the format and the material is well drafted and presented in readable and logical sequence.
My few remarks, Mr. Chairman, are really going to be in the nature of half a dozen questions which I wish to ask the minister. Will the minister, when he speaks, tell the committee what is the difference between trade and commerce? This has always been a rather intriguing question in my mind when the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce come before this committee. So far as the dictionary is concerned, I can find very little distinction. I wonder why the department is named, trade and commerce. There must be some reason for it. This is a question which arises out of my native curiosity.
I should like to direct the minister's attention to an item that appeared in the Globe and Mail of February 28 which, incidentally, is my birthday. It is entitled, "Canada doing little to meet challenge from trade blocs", and was written by Bruce Macdonald. I shall quote from it briefly and then I want to put a number of questions to the minister:
Despite the problems created for Canada from increasingly intense foreign competition, at home and abroad and from radically changing trade patterns resulting from the creation of new
Supply-Trade and Commerce economic blocs, so far there have been few changes in Canadian policy to meet the challenge. That these developments do have serious implications to this country, there is little doubt, deputy trade and commerce minister James Roberts emphasized in a Montreal speech today.
I would not be surprised if he were present in this building today.
"Economic decisions are now being taken by governments and businessmen in the free world which are far-reaching and which will have a profound effect on the future economic well-being of all Canadians," he asserted.
There is another paragraph of this article which I should like to quote. Mr. Roberts is a man of great experience whose opinion is highly regarded. He is reported as saying:
Mr. Roberts, who plays a key role in the development of policies to meet the challenge facing the country, provided no prescriptions of his own. For the first time, however, he did disclose some of the findings of the trade mission of 13 prominent Canadian businessmen which he led on a tour of the six-nation common market countries of Europe last fall, findings which may hold a lesson for this country.
"It is apparent that a major contribution to the area's economic development has been achieved through the effective co-operation and co-ordination of labour, management and government," the businessmen concluded. "The current prosperity in the community (European economic community) has been greatly influenced by the development and application of economic planning-"
Just think of it, Mr. Chairman; economic planning. This is C.C.F. policy.
-in the individual countries. These plans are gradually being integrated in an over-all economic plan for the common market.
In order to provide goods at lower costs to meet increasing competition, these countries in the European economic community have decided to do some over-all planning, some integration and working together on the basis of co-operation. My second question is, will the minister tell the committee what is being done by his department to develop in Canada between the various groups mentioned similar economic planning, co-ordination and co-operation which, from recent information, have proven so successful in western Europe? I do not blame the minister because he is working within a set of circumstances that exist at the moment. We all know that the minister is very active, and he is doing the best he can as an individual. I feel we have unplanned production in Canada and that production is unrelated to planned marketing, co-ordination, investment policies and so on. Members of this group believe we are going to have continuing difficulties, and possibly greater difficulties, until we develop some system which provides for over-all economic planning, co-ordination and co-operation. I should like the minister to

Supply-Trade and Commerce tell the committee what is being done in that respect. This is my second question, Mr. Chairman.
The hon. member for Vancouver East made some reference to the importance to British Columbia of the export of primary products, particularly products of the forest, of the sea and of the land, including minerals, fruit and other commodities. This is a very important question in British Columbia because of the extent of our primary industries. While secondary industry can be developed to a certain degree in British Columbia, we must recognize that our economy is essentially based on the successful development of the primary industries. This is the reason there is so much interest in British Columbia in the development of overseas markets. In recent years there has been great interest in the development of markets in Pacific countries. In British Columbia, when there is a federal election-the hon. member for Vancouver East will bear me out on this-you will find Progressive Conservative candidates readily urging from the platform the recognition of red China. When these men come here, their voices are rather dim. This is due to the fact that in British Columbia they are voicing the opinions of the working people of that province.
My third question is, in view of the recent success in the sale of wheat to China and in the extension of our market in Indonesia as well as some other countries, would the minister tell the committee what his department is doing to obtain similar success in the sale of various Canadian forest products, products of the sea and soil, fruit, minerals and other commodities, to China and other Asiatic countries. I think the sale of this wheat is a very encouraging sign. I have heard that this sale will be increased in the near future. I certainly look forward to the minister making an announcement soon. We would like him to tell the committee what he is doing to obtain similar success-we do not expect everything to happen overnight-with respect to the other commodities I have mentioned.
Some years ago, in 1959, it was brought to the attention of this house that Alcan, a Canadian company, was not permitted to accept a million dollar order because the parent company in the United States said it was against United States foreign policy and interests. There was a good deal of protest at that time against this subsidiary's failure to recognize the fact that it was operating on Canadian soil and using Canadian national resources and Canadian labour to make these profits. At the same time the Globe and Mail of Friday, January 23, 1959, in an editorial under the heading "What Price Sovereignty?" had this to say:

What is the burning topic in Canada today? Unemployment. Yet a large company meekly permits the Americans (or its fear of the Americans) to impose unemployment upon us. And how easy it is for them. They don't have to say anything, they don't have to do anything. The company's concern over what they might say, what they might do is enough to paralyse it; enough to make it take actions directly contrary to Canada's own welfare, Canada's own prosperity, Canada's own interests.
I understand that the situation was taken up at that time and that there was some improvement and some adjustment.
My fourth question is this. Will the minister inform the committee whether there have been any incidents of this type in Canada since he has taken office. I refer to incidents with respect to a Canadian subsidiary of a United States parent company refusing to accept orders from China or other countries of similar political ideology, because of instructions from the parent company or because it was against the policy of the United States.
I have two more questions. I am sure the minister takes a great interest in all the sayings and writings of people who are interested in improving our trade and commerce in Canada at this time. I am sure his attention has been directed to a speech by Hugh Llewellyn Keenleyside who made some suggestions with respect to the improvement of our trade. There are many people making suggestions without much knowledge or experience. However, I read this speech very carefully because Dr. Keenleyside was a former deputy minister. He was in charge of the technical assistance program for Canada at the United Nations through one of its agencies and he is now chairman of the British Columbia power commission. He has bad a distinguished academic and administrative career. I therefore read with interest what he had to say. I am not going to read the article in full. I am just going to read one paragraph. It appeared in the Financial Post of May 7, 1960. It is entitled "He Charts a Fresh Course for Canada" and it reads in part as follows:
Hugh Llewellyn Keenleyside, in over 30 years of distinguished public service-both in Canada and with the United Nations-has rightfully gained a reputation as an able administrator and an imaginative policy-maker. Few Canadians, in short, deserve a better hearing. He says:
"We should work out a system of selective free trade with the selection based on the willingness of U.S. countries to allocate an appropriate portion of their total (North American) production to factories established in Canada.
"There is no reason why it should not be extended to any country that is willing to meet the basic qualification: The establishment of new factories in Canada and free access for its products to the consumer market of the other country."

Then The Province of May 10 had this to say in an editorial entitled "A Challenge to Canadian Ingenuity . .
Dr. Hugh L. Keenleyside's formula for "selective free trade" as an answer to Canada's increasing economic problems offers so many logical and practical features that no time should be lost in examining it more closely.
The steps suggested by the British Columbia power commission chairman and former United Nations' official... have received enough preliminary publicity and discussion to warrant an exhaustive and critical study by both government and private business.
We say both government and private business because the agreement and co-operation of both is manifestly necessary if anything is going to be done about this proposal. Neither government edict nor private business policy could, alone, bring about the desired result.
I am extremely pleased just to note in passing that even The Province is beginning to speak the language used by the C.C.F. over the years. It mentions the necessity for cooperation between government and private business in dealing with economic problems. We have advanced those views throughout the years in our development of what we call the theory of a mixed or dual economy.
My fifth question to the minister is this. Has he read of these proposals by Dr. Keen-leyside and has he given them his careful study and attention? If so, will he inform the committee as to his opinion of their practical nature and of the possibility, as a result of the application of Dr. Keenleyside's proposals, of improving somewhat our position with respect to trade and commerce in Canada and consequently the unemployment situation?
My sixth and last question is simply this. I was reading the departmental report in my office, especially one section of it that is of great interest to me, namely the section that deals with small business. It was established largely to gather information, to offer advice, to publish literature and to undertake activities of that type. It is of interest to hon. members and I quite frequently receive letters making inquiries about this branch. On occasion people confuse the branch with the organization under the bill that provides for loans to small business enterprises and their improvement.
When the minister replies, will he give the committee some illustration of the work this small business branch is doing at the present time? I should like to have something a little bit more detailed than what one reads in the report. I should like to know about the literature that is being published or the pamphlets and whether this literature or this publicity is available to members. Can he give us some idea of the nature of the inquiries, of the number of small business firms that have been

Supply-Trade and Commerce served by advice, by literature or by information since the establishment of this branch in this department?
With those few brief remarks I conclude my words at this time, Mr. Chairman.

Trade and commerce historically have been the physical body of the nation. If national idealism and principles are the spirit of the nation, then trading is its blood and commerce its bone, and sinew. I may be pardoned for saying that I come from a province which for hundreds of years has depended for its very existence on trading. In the days before we entered confederation and became a part of the Canadian family, Newfoundland exported everything it produced. It imported practically everything it consumed. Since confederation we still export practically everything we produce and we buy practically all we consume from the mainland of Canada, most of it, of course, from the industrial provinces of central Canada.
If I may make a personal observation, I should like to say that I grew up in Catalina, a seaport on the east coast of Newfoundland. As a boy, in the days of sail, when our own ships carried our own products to the foreign markets, our horizons were Spain and Italy, Portugal and Greece and the islands of the Caribbean. If you walked down the streets at any time, you would rub shoulders with sailors who were just home from "across" as we referred to foreign markets, or who were getting ready to sail to foreign markets with fish. The means of shipping has changed and steam and diesel power and vessels of other registry carry our products today but the pattern of trade remains the same as it was. Hence trade and commerce is of vital importance to us in Newfoundland. It is important to those of my constituents who are fishermen, it is important to those of my constituents who are loggers, and to all who work and depend upon the production of pulp and paper for their livelihood. It is also important to the growing number of my constituents who are engaged in mining. Thus the Department of Trade and Commerce, to us in Newfoundland, the Atlantic provinces and all Canada, is one of the most important departments of government. This is because it is the basic department of government. I wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment as head of this department, although in a way I have lost a constituent from Gander.
I wish to speak particularly of the position relative to the marketing of salt codfish. I think I can say with assurance that Canada is not holding her own in this sphere.

Supply-Trade and Commerce Certainly the number of nations now engaged in fishing off our coasts, and the increasing pressure of competition from them- competition which we are feeling in our historic markets-indicates that we have slipped rather than made headway. I have felt for some time that insufficient attention has been paid to the selling of salt codfish. I believe there are not enough trade representatives detailed to sell this product.
The minister's department has some capable men who are doing very good work in this respect, but they are too few. I feel, also, that the fish business is not receiving the proportion of attention which it needs. I believe that an intense effort should be directed toward the sale of fish, the promotion of fish sales and the development of new markets. I believe that more officials are needed to get out in the various countries, promote fish sales and interest new customers. We should not be content to do business merely with our old customers.
We must keep our old customers, of course. We must sell them larger quantities of fish, if we can; but we must keep a weather eye open for new markets. In this respect I suggest that the potential of Africa as a market for Canadian fish should be explored. I think too, that the productivity council may be interested in the developing of new products, because it is possible that in order to develop new markets some change may have to be made in the type of product we are now offering for sale to the world.
If we are to obtain new markets and develop old ones it is perhaps important that we pay more attention to either new developments or perhaps a greater production of one type of salt codfish over another.
Certainly it seems that we are suffering a loss of sales by not producing more of what is generally known as light salted shore fish. In the past, light salted shore fish has been produced largely by hand labour, and sun dried. The cost of production is high. Heavily salted fish can be produced by artificial driers, or finished by them. The cost of production is cut down in this case.
It is very possible that we are producing, proportionately with the volume of sales now being made, too much of the heavy salted article and not sufficient of the fight salted article.
However, in order to produce the light salted article economically it is necessary that a means of artificial production be evolved, and this is certainly possible. I mention this in passing because I know that in these modern days it is unrealistic to expect the old, traditional method of producing fish to be used successfully.


I do not think I should go into further detail on these estimates, but I will have something to say about this matter when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries come up later. However, I do think this has a direct bearing upon our trade and our trade potential.
It is possible that by not producing enough of this particular type of fish we are rapidly losing a potential market, because if a product which people have been used to buying over the years is cut off, or is withheld long enough, the demand will soon cease to exist. I ask the minister to bear this matter in mind.
I now come back to the question of the sale of fish. The fact is that Newfoundland and all the Atlantic provinces feel-and, I believe, justifiably-that there is not enough attention and serious effort put into the building up of the fish trade. It is felt there could be more effort in this direction.
Perhaps if the same attention were given to the development of trade in fish as is given to the sale of grain, for instance, the position of the industry would be vastly improved. Certainly we have an immense wealth of food in our Canadian waters. We have the product with which trade began in the new world.
The minister is undoubtedly aware of the fact that when John Cabot discovered Canada, on sighting Cape Bonavista on St. John's day, 1497, he discovered that the waters were full of fish. At the time, according to tradition, John Cabot was looking for gold and precious stones for Henry VII who had, shall I say, an orthodox sense of values. But John Cabot discovered fish instead of gold and jewels, and fish proved to be a greater source of wealth to England than gold or jewels would have been.
It is a matter of historic record that one year after the discovery of Canada, in 1498, British merchants were outfitting fishing ships and sending them to Canadian waters, to the waters of the new world, to develop a fishing trade. Pretty soon they were followed by the French, the Portuguese and the Spaniards. Competition became keen, and that pattern has continued to exist. These historic competitors are still fishing in the waters off the coast of Canada. They have been joined by many other nations today, including Russia. They have been developing and building up their fish trade to an extent perhaps never known before in history. They recognize the value of developing this great source of food.
Certainly we in Canada, where trading in fish began, can meet and beat this competition. The methods, the means and the brains all exist. It is just a matter of focusing them

on a very real problem. This is not only a Newfoundland problem, but it is an Atlantic provinces and a Canadian problem. We in the Atlantic provinces are among the best customers of central Canada. Newfoundland was at one time the third best customer of Canada. What she buys today from the mainland of Canada is very difficult to assess, but it would be more than she bought prior to confederation.
If it requires money, if it means the employing of more trade secretaries to increase our trade in fish, to build up the ancient trade and commerce of the new world, it will be a sound investment because it will mean the building up not only of the economy of Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces but the creation of wealth in which all Canada would share. I ask the minister to take a very close and sympathetic look at the development of trade and commerce as it affects the fish industry and in particular the salt codfish industry. I should like him at the appropriate time to tell this committee what the department may be doing in this respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Trade and Commerce is fortunate in having the dynamic leadership of the new minister. Trade, as everyone knows, is the lifeblood of our nation, and I wish to speak principally today of just one product, oil.
We have to balance our trade with the other countries of the world and there is nothing which could balance the trade of Canada quicker than the development of our oil resources. I represent the great district of Athabasca and it should now be well known, if it is not already well known, that contained within the Athabasca district alone is the largest known deposit of crude oil on this planet. It has been conservatively estimated that anywhere from three hundred to five hundred billion barrels of oil at present lie in the sand hills there and are available whenever we are ready to take them out.
I should like to bring this to the attention of our new minister because one of these days the supply of world crude oil may suddenly be cut off from us. If proper steps are taken now-and I mean now-to tap this well nigh unlimited source, Canada and possibly the free world may be saved in time of crisis. But we have to get this plant going. It has to be financed. It has to be encouraged by the provision of both federal and provincial money. I think it would be an eternal disgrace to us if we left this, the largest oil deposit in the world, untapped and unready to be used.
It has been erroneously said on many occasions that this oil could not be taken out 90205-6-261
Supply-Trade and Commerce of the sand or that it would not be economic to take it out. Neither of these statements is correct. We have a well known process now for extracting this oil and there is only one bottleneck, namely the development of a suitable market for the product. But we have that market here in Canada if we were to take the proper steps to utilize it. The Montreal district alone uses in the neighbourhood of 80,000 barrels of heavy industrial fuel oil a day and I understand from properly informed source that if we had the benefit of this market in Athabasca we would go into full production. I know that we have at the present time very extensive plans in co-operation with our United States neighbours with reference to oil but I think we should take a long look at this situation and lay plans now for the development of the industry here.
We shall have to do it sooner or later. I do not think we want to be caught without oil at any time when it is physically available to us now. Cities Service Oil Company have a pilot plant going now at a cost of $1,500,000. They are working on an oil face which is very limited in extent but they could produce from this one cliff alone 80,000 barrels of oil a day for 60 years without moving their plant. Such figures are astronomical and it is hard to understand-the people up in my area certainly find it hard to understand-why more attention is not paid to these enormous deposits. We have the fresh water there. We have the oil itself to supply the fuel needs. We have the people of Canada willing to get in there and work, and I think we can expect the full co-operation of the Department of Trade and Commerce as soon as the province of Alberta gives the go-ahead to these farsighted and progressive companies which are doing and wish to do the exploratory work.
This tar sand country is not only rich in oil but it has great potential for the delivery of many important by-products including sulphur, tar, salt and the crystal clear sand which remains after the process is completed; sand which would provide an excellent basis for a glass industry. I see the day when northern Alberta will become another Ruhr. All it will take is the planning and the financing which the companies concerned have already started-a progressive plan which they are looking to government at both federal and provincial levels to assist.
I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-21 to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).
He said: When the two-day debate on this bill concluded last February approximately 20 speakers had supported the opposite view to the one proposed in this measure. In fact, a clear majority of the members of the House of Commons had indicated their opposition to the bill and Gallup polls which were taken at the time when the debate took place indicated that a slight majority of the people of Canada shared that view. It is my purpose today to attempt to review the 20 speeches made by the retentionist group and to reply to the questions and objections which were raised to this bill.
I should like to put on the record certain information such as the Gallup poll results, which I mentioned earlier, and other information, in particular that dealing with the state of Delaware. The state of Delaware, as you will recall, sir, was mentioned in the debate last year as being a state which has most recently abolished capital punishment in the United States. One particularly interesting piece of information which I should like to place on the record today deals with a letter written to Senator Fred Farr, of the state of California. It will be recalled that about the time of the debate on my bill last year the Chessman case was very much in the news and the state of California was contemplating a debate on the merits of capital punishment at that time. Senator Farr apparently was a member of the legislative committee of the senate of the state of California and he wrote to the governor of the state of Delaware. The interesting thing about the questions he asked is that these are the questions or, if you like, the doubts which obviously were in the minds of hon. members of this house during the debate last year and during other debates in previous sessions. This letter written by Governor Caleb Beggs to Senator Farr, reads as follows:
I acknowledge receipt of your telegram of March 7 which was received here on March 8. I regret that through a misunderstanding here a reply to your telegram was not sent for your hearing on March 9. However, I am only too pleased to answer your telegram and do so as follows:
1. Has abolition of death penalty increased homicide rate in your state?
The answer is as follows:
Abolition has not increased the homicide rate in Delaware. Abolition became effective April 2, 1958. A comparison for 12 months prior to abolition with 12 months after showed no change in

the homicide rate. The number of criminal homicides for 1958 was 12; for 1959 it had dropped to seven.
This, Mr. Speaker, of course, deals with the anticipated rise in the homicide rate which certain people suggest will follow abolition.
The second question reads:
Does lack of capital punishment add to danger of police and other peace officers?
The answer is:
There is no evidence whatsoever to show that attacks upon police officers have changed because of the absence of capital punishment. Actually in Delaware throughout the years we have had very few attacks upon police officers and there has been no change in this situation. After reviewing the evidence prior to the passage of the bill the superintendents of the state police and certain other police forces in the state in our larger cities took the position they would not oppose the passage of the bill for abolition.
The third question reads:
Is there any substantial movement for restoration of death penalty?
The answer is:
There is no movement whatsoever.
The fourth question reads:
Has absence of death penalty made it harder or easier to obtain jury convictions in murder cases?
The answer is:
We have had only a few murder trials since abolition. It is our belief that the jury is less reluctant to bring in a first degree verdict where the facts warrant it.
The fifth question reads:
Has absence of death penalty in any way increased danger to public safety?
The answer is no.
The sixth question reads:
Does absence of death penalty create security problem in prisons?
The answer is no.
The seventh question reads:
Based on your experience, would you recommend abolition of death penalty by California?
The answer is:
Our experience of two years since abolition has shown a decrease in the homicide rate. Based solely upon our experience, therefore, we can recommend abolition. Delaware's experience follows the pattern shown in all the studies that the removal of the death penalty does not increase the homicide rate.
I trust that the above answers your inquiry and will be of service to you.
And so on.
This, Mr. Speaker, is another piece of the growing pile of evidence in answer to the understandable questions and doubts which are and still remain in the public mind.
The first hon. member who spoke against this bill in the debate last year was the

hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). In the early part of his remarks he said as reported at page 1195 of Hansard of February 18, 1960:
I completely reject the arguments they have put forward.
He continued.
It is rather surprising to me that people so far from public opinion could find themselves in the House of Commons.
This question of public opinion is a very interesting one indeed and particularly when you examine the trend of public opinion over the last few years. Public opinion polls were taken on this subject by the Canadian institute of public opinion in 1943, 1953, 1958 and 1960, which as I indicated before was shortly after the second day's debate of this bill last year. This was the question put:
Some people say we should do away altogether with capital punishment; that is, executing a person for murder. Do you think we should or should not abolish capital punishment?
In 1943, 18 per cent replied that capital punishment should be abolished. In 1953, the figure had risen to 22 per cent; in 1958, it had risen to 33 per cent; and in 1960, it has risen to 41 per cent. Those who would retain capital punishment amounted to 73 per cent in 1943; 71 per cent in 1953; 52 per cent in 1958; and it was down to 51 per cent in 1960. The "no opinion" factor makes up the remainder. For the record, in 1943, they amounted to 9 per cent; in 1953, to 7 per cent; in 1958, to 15 per cent; and in 1960, to 8 per cent.
The indications are clear, Mr. Speaker, not only in these public opinion polls but in the actions of juries and in other manifestations across the country that there is a growing body of persons in this country who favour the abolition of capital punishment.

The bill of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, which was patterned closely on the English homicide act of 1957, is a move toward abolition and an attempt to reduce the application of the death penalty.
Before hon. members become too enamoured of the British experience, I should like to point out in passing that some serious difficulties have been encountered in England with this measure which, as hon. members well know, attempts to set up five categories of murder which are defined as capital murder, all other grounds being punishable by life imprisonment. One category, for instance, is the committing of a murder in the process of a theft. Another category involves a murder using a gun or a bomb. Another category is a second murder. Another category is killing a policeman or prison guard, and so on.
This attempt to stop part way along the road to abolition has produced some serious contradictions. One of these was described by Gerald Gardiner, Q.C., who happens to be the head of the British society for the abolition of capital punishment. In a speech recently he had this to say:
For instance, if a man comes home and finds his wife with another man and picks up the nearest weapon to murder her, it is a capital offence if that weapon happens to be a gun, but a noncapital offence if it is a hatchet.
I might add there, Mr. Speaker, that presumably if the type of crime is determined by the weapon chosen a man could boil his wife in oil, strap her to a board in the style of "The Perils of Pauline" and run her into a buzz saw or use any other sort of peculiar and unusual method to commit murder and if he adopts any of these quaint methods he cannot be hanged whereas if he happens to use a gun he will hang. Mr. Gardiner goes on to say:
If someone rapes a woman and steals her handbag, it is a capital offence; if he does not steal her handbag, it is non-capital.
Contradictions and difficulties have evolved in reaching and determining the point in the degree of culpability of murder at which a person shall be hanged. When you draw that line a case which qualifies for capital punishment will differ so infinitesimally from one just on the other side of the line that for all practical purposes there is no real difference.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway went on to say, as found on page 1195 of Hansard for February 18, 1960:
-having regard to the protection of our police officers, surely common sense would tell us that, if a man has committed a crime where he is going to be committed to life imprisonment, is being apprehended by a police officer and is armed, there is going to be the temptation for him, knowing that he can escape, knowing that if he shoots the police officer he can be no worse off than he was before. Surely it is going to act as a deterrent to that man if he knows he is going to be hanged, something which is considerably more abhorrent to him than is life imprisonment in most cases.
This is one of these apparently attractive arguments held by those who would retain the death penalty. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and others have tried to get inside the mind of the potential murderer and have reached certain conclusions about what his reaction will or will not be. I am certainly voicing no suggestion that I can make any better evaluation of what goes on inside a criminal's mind, but I would say to the hon. members who hold this view that if they examine the 42 jurisdictions -I mean countries and states within countries where capital punishment is a matter of state jurisdiction-they will find that when capital punishment has been abolished the incidence of murder, as indicated in the letter of the governor of the state of Delaware, has not risen suddenly.
