I believe that one of the things the public do not like about our present system is the hanging, and perhaps some other method of carrying out the death penalty should be instituted-
I suggest that this particular facet of the argument is in one sense beside the point and certainly in another sense it is inconsistent. Those who favour the retention of the death penalty by means of hanging put forward the argument that the menacing quality of death by this means forms the essential deterrent. That is the deterrent argument, but if hanging is something which is unacceptable to many people I cannot understand why a person advocating the retention of the death penalty would want to lessen the menacing character of that deterrent. It seems to me that the hon. member is on two sides of the argument at the same time.

The next speaker in the debate to whom I wish to refer was the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau). I must say that in preparing my speech one suggestion occurred to me which I might throw in at this point. I suggest it might be more desirable to have one completely English Hansard and another completely in French. I find that skipping backward and forward between translations and coming back to the place where I started is difficult. The hon. member for Dollard made this statement, as found on page 1204 of Hansard for February 18, 1960:
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, if public opinion is divided about the abolition of capital punishment, we should be even more cautious about this matter than we have been in the case of a Canadian flag.
Without meaning to be facetious, I would say it would be hard to be more cautious than that. The hon. member went on to say that a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate was established to consider the advisability of abolishing capital punishment. The decision of that committee, as you know, Mr. Speaker, was that for the time being it should be retained. I came across some information concerning that decision which I found rather unusual. Apparently it is the only committee in the history of the House of Commons to take its final vote on the basis of telegrams from all parts of the country. However, the committee certainly reflected public opinion at that time which indicated, as I said, that 71 per cent of the people of Canada favoured that proposition.
References were made to the fact that a private member should have brought forward such a bill. The hon. member for Dollard made such a reference and it was repeated by a number of his colleagues in the Liberal party. It seems to me that this attitude overlooks the essential function of parliament as a debating forum. Surely the debate that took place on the bill caused considerable discussion both in the house and throughout the country and as a result the government, whose function it is to assess and evaluate public opinion, was assisted tremendously.
The hon. member also made the statement that we must not forget the victims or the dependents of the victims. This was a trend in the debate which the hon. member for Dollard started and which gathered force as the debate continued on the second day. Speaker after speaker called out for sympathy, consideration and compassion for the victims of murder and their dependents. Certainly, the impression I gained in view of the rather loud applause which accompanied these continual references was that those of us who favoured the abolition of capital

punishment were lacking in sympathy, understanding and appreciation of the plight of those people who remained.
I would remind the hon. member for Dollard, as well as other hon. members, that the first words I uttered in this debate were that I was not prompted by any lack of sympathy for the unfortunate victims of murder and their dependents, nor was I overly sympathetic to the accused. This rather unfortunate trend in the debate certainly was not accompanied by any positive suggestions from the retentionists to do something about the widows and orphans of the victims of murder.
I should like to put a suggestion before the house and the record will show that it was an abolitionist who put forward this proposal. A proposal has been circulated in England in these terms. In the case of murder, why should not the person responsible for the damage to the family of the victim be required to pay compensation in the same way as he would be if he were driving a car and, through negligence, killed somebody? The courts could decide that certain damages would be awarded to the victim or his dependents. It seems to me there is much merit in a proposal to have those found guilty of murder sentenced to life imprisonment in an institution where some money earning occupation could be undertaken. The money earned could be placed in a fund from which could be drawn money to assist, in a practical way, the victims and their dependents who may be in need.
Another factor worthy of consideration is that a fund could also be provided from which assistance could be given to the accused's family and children who may be in need. As I say, I am not putting this forward in any concrete form, but it seems to me this proposal is constructive and demonstrates some real interest and concern for the victims of murder and their dependents.
The hon. member went on to quote from the Bible. Many members on both sides of this question quoted from both the Old and the New Testaments in support of the views that they took. I do not want to make any reference to those questions now, but I would refer hon. members to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who, after studying the representations on both sides of this question, found an equal number of biblical quotations which were applicable to each side of the argument.

Evans was a man with a mental age of 10J years. He could neither read nor write. The strong suggestion of the defence and others who inquired into this matter was that the language and pattern of those confessions were dictated by the police to suit facts of which they had knowledge at that time.

I should like to agree with the hon. member for Charlotte. We have an impressive judicial system, but it is a system made up of human beings. There are impressive guarantees in our system, but as long as human beings are human beings, mistakes will be made; and mistakes have been made.

The suggestion is that they are restrained from committing murder only because of the existence of the rope. If this seemingly plausible argument is sound, surely if the deterrent and the threat of the rope is removed the incidence of murder will increase.

I offer again the accumulated evidence of 100 years, for this matter is no

longer in the experimental stage. I submit that we are hanging persons for murder, and unless we can demonstrate the necessity for so doing I find it difficult to understand why support for it continues.
The hon. member for Calgary South made reference to certain increases in the crime rate in the interval when capital punishment was suspended. He quoted a figure of 14.8 per cent at one point during that interval. I am prepared to accept that statistic as being possible but I should also like to refer him and the house to the pattern of the crime rate during the 18-month period before abolition, the period during abolition and the period immediately after abolition. I think the figures are 285 before, 260 during and 310 or so following. This indicates that although there may have been a slight increase within the period, as an experimental period it supported the abolitionist contention.
The hon. member concluded his speech by making reference to the theme that those of us who would abolish capital punishment are not concerned with the victims, and an impressive statement it was. Again I would remind the house that all through those debates the only constructive efforts which were put forward to provide in a tangible way for an approach to this question came from those who would abolish the death penalty.
The hon. member went on to say that we were being asked to abolish a provision which had made Canada relatively free of crime as compared with other countries. Here we come to an old argument. The hon. member says we should retain capital punishment because our crime rate is low. Persons writing to me from Toronto and Montreal where crime rates have increased say we cannot abolish the death penalty because crime rates are increasing. As I said last year in the debate, one cannot have it both ways. It cannot be argued that we should retain the death penalty because the crime rate is decreasing while at the same time arguing that we should retain it now that the crime rate is going up.
One other matter which I wanted to cover was raised by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) who also had a motion or a bill on the order paper; it may still be there. The hon. member had this to say. He said that we had in Canada partially abolished capital punishment, and then he went on to suggest that we should consider leaving the judges free to inflict the death penalty or to condemn those accused to life sentences according to the gravity or the circumstances of the crime.
It seems to me that this proposal fails on two important grounds. It fails on the one hand because it attempts to pass the buck- in other words it asks somebody other than

Criminal Code
parliament to render a decision on capital punishment. The second shortcoming of the proposal is this. It seems to me that after a relatively short period-a year or so-a pattern would emerge. Certain judges would be known as hanging judges and certain others would be known as non-hanging judges. It seems to me that the variations in the equal treatment of persons who appear before the courts are sufficient at present without adding this extra factor where the decision as to whether a man lives or dies would depend on the judge selected to try the case. I think on these two grounds the proposition fails.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I preface it by saying it deals with the indication in the speech from the throne that the minister himself will bring in some amendment regarding capital punishment. I wonder what the hon. member's thoughts are concerning the probable comments of his colleagues who were either vehemently opposed to or in favour of capital punishment. How does he think they will vote when the minister presents his bill?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
I am not prepared to speak for anybody in this house apart from myself, but if that bill develops so as to limit the application of the death penalty I would certainly support it as a measure moving
towards abolition. I pointed out earlier in my remarks some of the difficulties which have been encountered in the United Kingdom in attempting to stop half way; but it strikes me as reminiscent of a young fellow in our gang as a youngster who every time the score was going against him in a ball game took his ball and went home. I would not like to be in that position. I would support any move toward abolition. I feel that the public attitude and public opinion on this matter will ultimately be such that we shall see capital punishment abolished.
